There’s no limit on how angry you’re *allowed* to feel. The better question is whether holding onto the anger is doing anything for you. If you want clarity, you could ask at a quiet moment: “Hey, when I was running up that day, were you already unable to stop? I wasn’t sure how that works.” Or you can leave it alone and be as friendly—or as businesslike—as you feel like being.

The online name-calling isn’t useful feedback. But neither is telling yourself, “I’m supposed to hate this guy.” You can still wish he’d waited without making yourself stay mad until he apologizes.

You’re not an asshole for being angry, and you don’t owe the driver jokes or small talk. Paying your fare and keeping to yourself was a perfectly reasonable response. But you don’t owe your past self a grudge, either. Laughing with him doesn’t mean you were wrong to be upset.

I’d separate **“he saw me and didn’t wait”** from **“he wanted to strand me.”** The first may be true; the second is harder to know. You were still approaching the stop, and picking someone up at a red light may be against the rules or unsafe. Other drivers doing it doesn’t establish that this driver could or should have. It still makes sense that it felt personal when someone you regularly chatted with drove on.

If it’s still bothering you, you could ask at a quiet moment, “Hey, remember when I was running for the bus? Are you allowed to wait when someone’s almost at the stop?” You might get an explanation even if you don’t get an apology. Or you can let it go without deciding he was right.

The online name-calling isn’t useful. There *is* a fair point underneath the criticism: feeling angry in the moment is one thing; being mad at yourself months later for not staying angry is another. You don’t have to keep the anger alive to prove the incident mattered.

Yes, you’d be the asshole **if you threw them out without her permission**. Thinking the pants are past their prime is fine. Deciding they’re gone after she’s made it clear she wants to keep them would turn a low-stakes disagreement into a trust issue.

It makes sense that it seemed normal if you grew up watching your mum do it. (The divorce is a funny postscript, not evidence that the pants did it.) Your girlfriend pointing out which of *your* things she’d toss is a good gut check: you’d probably want the final say, too.

Go shopping together if you both want to. If she loves the fit, you could offer to help replace the elastic instead. And if she just wants to keep wearing her ancient weekend pants? That’s a perfectly good ending, too.

Yes, you’d be the asshole if you threw them out without her permission. You’re allowed to think the pants are past saving; she’s allowed to keep wearing them. You’ve brought it up, she’s heard you, and she’s made her choice. They can go on as long as she wants them to.

Shopping together sounds fun if you both want to, but buying new pants doesn’t mean the old ones have to go. If the elastic bothers *her*, you could offer to get it replaced.

And your parents’ divorce isn’t evidence against a trouser policy. Seeing your mum do it explains why it felt normal to you; it doesn’t make it a rule you have to carry into your own relationship.

Yes, you’d be in the wrong if you threw them out without her permission. The pants may be well past the point where *you’d* retire them, but she still wears them every weekend. You’d be taking away something she uses, not doing her a favor. And it could make her wonder what else you’d decide to toss on her behalf.

It makes sense that this seemed normal if you saw your mum do it. That explains the instinct; it doesn’t make it a good rule for your household. And there’s no reason to read anything about your parents’ divorce into the pants.

It sounds like you two already found a better way forward: laugh about the stuff you both hang on to, go shopping if you both want to, and let each person decide what to retire. If she likes the old pair but hates the busted waistband, you could offer to get the elastic replaced. If she’s happy with them as they are, let the pants keep their weekend shift.

You’re allowed to be angry, and you’re not an asshole for switching to a polite, business-only relationship with the driver. You don’t owe him jokes or smiles. But you don’t owe yourself a grudge, either. Laughing with him doesn’t mean you’ve decided what happened was okay.

I’d separate **“he saw me and didn’t wait”** from **“he deliberately stranded me.”** The first sounds plausible from what you describe. The second implies he meant to leave you in the lurch, and you don’t know that. Ten feet feels like nothing when you’re the one running, but a driver may already be committed to pulling out, and a red light isn’t a boarding stop. Other drivers waiting for you explains why you expected him to; it doesn’t establish that he was obliged to.

If it still bothers you, you could ask at a quiet moment, “That day I was running up to the stop, were you already committed to leaving?” You might get an explanation, though not necessarily an apology. Or you can just keep things cordial and let yourself laugh when something’s funny. Neither choice requires you to pretend you weren’t upset.

The online name-calling isn’t useful feedback. The fair question underneath it is whether one frustrating incident still deserves this much of your attention. It sounds like your anger had already started to fade on its own. That’s not a failure to stand up for yourself.

**Soft YTA—not for being annoyed, but for blaming the neighbors for the ticket when you don’t know they called.** Their address on the ticket tells you which driveway the officer cited, not who reported it or whether anyone did.

Your girlfriend was trying to be considerate by letting the car overhang your driveway rather than theirs. But depending on your local bylaws, parking too close to a driveway can still be a violation even if the car doesn’t physically block it. If she thinks the officer cited the wrong driveway or got the clearance wrong, she can check the rule and contest the ticket with photos or measurements.

A heads-up would’ve been neighborly if they did call, and it makes sense that you’d have preferred one. But letting other things slide doesn’t mean they owe you the same. I’d have her park across the street for now and, if you want to clear the air, ask without accusing: “Hey, we got a ticket by the driveways. Has where we’ve been parking made it harder for you to get in or out?”

**Mild YTA—not for being annoyed, but for blaming the neighbor without knowing what happened.**

If your girlfriend was only blocking *your* driveway and you were okay with it, she wasn’t being inconsiderate to the neighbor. But your permission doesn’t necessarily make the parking legal, and the neighbor’s address on the ticket doesn’t prove they called. It may just be how the officer recorded the location.

Even if they did call, it’s fair to wish they’d knocked first. But letting other things slide doesn’t mean they owe you the same, especially if they thought the car made it harder to get in or out.

Check the exact violation and the local driveway-clearance rule. If the ticket identifies the wrong driveway or you have evidence the car was parked legally, contest it. Either way, I’d go back to parking across the street rather than turn one ticket into a feud.

**Mild YTA for blaming the neighbors, not for being annoyed about the ticket.** It would’ve been neighborly to give you a heads-up, and I get why you wish they had. But the address on the ticket doesn’t prove they called, and even if they did, you don’t know whether the car looked like it was encroaching from their side.

Your girlfriend was trying to be considerate by leaving their driveway clear. Still, your permission to block *your* driveway may not make it legal, and some places require clearance beside a driveway even if the car doesn’t cross the opening. Check the exact bylaw and the ticket’s stated location. If the facts don’t match the violation, contest it; otherwise, she should go back to parking across the street.

As for the things you’ve let slide, it’s understandable that this feels one-sided, but that doesn’t mean they owed you a pass. If you want to clear the air, ask without accusing: “We got a ticket there and thought we were leaving your driveway clear. Was the car in your way?”

You’re not an asshole for being disappointed. You don’t see each other often, and it’s frustrating that neither place worked out this weekend. But you’re being unfair if you’re treating her decision as a betrayal or telling her the friendship isn’t worth keeping.

I can see why it feels like a double standard: her roommate gets to host her boyfriend, and you’re the one asked not to come. That’s worth discussing if it becomes a pattern. But one request about a shared space isn’t enough to judge the whole friendship. Your girlfriend also has to live with her roommate after the weekend is over, so it’s reasonable for her to care about keeping things cordial. You’re accepting your parents’ limits on hosting this weekend; give her some room to navigate hers, too.

You could say, “I was really looking forward to seeing you, and I think I took my disappointment out on you. I get why you didn’t want to push it. Could we meet somewhere for a few hours, or pick our next weekend now?” If visits keep falling through because her roommate’s guests get priority, talk with your girlfriend about what a fair guest arrangement would look like—not whether she should drop the friendship.

**Not an asshole for being disappointed. You’d be in the wrong if you treated your girlfriend like she let you down by not pushing back on her roommate.**

You rarely get to see each other, and it’s frustrating that the roommate gets to host her boyfriend on the one weekend your place isn’t available. It’s fair to want a more reciprocal guest arrangement if this becomes a pattern. But you don’t have to agree that four people sharing a bathroom is a big deal to understand why your girlfriend would rather not turn one weekend into a conflict with someone she lives with. And one inconsiderate request, if that’s what it was, isn’t enough to conclude the friendship isn’t worth keeping.

You don’t have to hide that you’re upset. Just make clear what you’re upset *about*: “I miss you, and I’m bummed we might not get this weekend together. I don’t want you to feel like I’m blaming you. Could we meet up during the day, or pick our next weekend now?”

If her roommate regularly expects to host while asking your girlfriend not to, that’s a good reason for them to talk about guest expectations. For this weekend, focus on finding time together rather than on whether your girlfriend should have fought harder for the visit.

**You’re not an asshole for being disappointed. But I think you’re being a little unfair to your girlfriend about what that disappointment means.**

Four people sharing a bathroom for a weekend might be no big deal to you, and it’s fair to wonder why the roommate’s boyfriend gets to visit while you’re asked not to. But one inconvenient request doesn’t mean the roommate is a bad friend. Your girlfriend shares a living space with her, and it’s reasonable that she’d rather accommodate her this once than turn it into a dispute. You’re also respecting your parents’ request not to host this weekend, so both of you are working around the preferences of people you live with.

You don’t need to hide that you’re upset. The distinction is between “I’m bummed we won’t get our weekend together” and “You’re wrong for not pushing back.” If you’ve been making it feel like the second, you can reset: “I was really looking forward to seeing you, and I think I took my frustration out on you a bit. Could we still meet up during the day, or pick another weekend now?”

If the roommate regularly expects her own boyfriend to visit while asking your girlfriend not to host you, that’s worth a conversation about a fair guest arrangement. One weekend isn’t enough to conclude there’s a pattern.

Yes—if you dismiss her request because she seems better now, you’d be making a mistake. **Take her request seriously and help her get an initial appointment.** That doesn’t mean committing to years of expensive therapy. It means giving her a chance to talk with someone who can help her figure out what she needs.

It’s encouraging that she seems calmer and that you haven’t seen her hurt herself lately. But what you see from the outside isn’t the whole picture, and her past self-harm makes it especially important to listen. Turning down a group in middle school doesn’t mean she doesn’t want one-on-one support now. Therapy also isn’t a verdict on your parenting, and what her dad needed after his experiences doesn’t tell you what she needs after hers.

You could say: “I’m glad you asked me. I thought that because you seemed better, you felt better, but I don’t want to assume. You don’t have to tell me everything to deserve help. Let’s figure out what we can afford.” Her pediatrician is a good starting point for an assessment and referrals. You can also ask about insurance coverage, sliding-scale fees, or school counseling as a bridge while you look.

Given her history, ask calmly and directly whether she’s been hurting herself recently or thinking about suicide. If she says yes, seek prompt professional guidance. If she has a plan or intent to act, has seriously injured herself, or can’t stay safe, stay with her and seek emergency help right away.

Cost is a real constraint. The distinction is between **“We may not be able to afford the first option”** and **“You don’t need help.”** You can be honest about the first without deciding the second for her.

Yes, I think you’d be wrong to dismiss her request. That doesn’t mean you’re a bad parent or that you have to commit to expensive weekly therapy. It means taking her seriously and helping her find a first appointment or another accessible source of support.

Your daughter may look calmer and still be struggling in ways you can’t see. Puberty may have played a role, but it doesn’t explain away her past self-harm or tell you how she feels now. A school group she didn’t want to attend then is different from individual help she’s asking for now. And your husband’s experience doesn’t tell you what your daughter needs. Therapy isn’t something she needs to prove she was abused—or is “unwell enough”—to deserve.

You could say: “I’m glad you asked me. I assumed you were feeling better because things seemed calmer, but I realize I don’t know how it’s been for you. You don’t have to tell me everything to get my help. Let’s figure out what we can afford.”

Given her history, ask calmly and directly whether she’s been hurting herself recently or having thoughts of suicide. If she says she might act on those thoughts or can’t stay safe, stay with her and seek emergency or crisis help right away. If she reports recent self-harm without immediate danger, contact her pediatrician promptly for guidance.

For cost, start with her pediatrician, school counselor, or insurer if you have one. Ask about an initial assessment, sliding-scale providers, or community youth services. You don’t have to settle the question of long-term therapy today. The next step is to listen and help her get assessed, rather than deciding from the outside that she’s fine.

You’re not wrong to worry about the cost, but I wouldn’t turn down her request. She has a history of hurting herself, and now she’s asking for help in her own words. That’s worth taking seriously even if she seems calmer and hasn’t hurt herself recently.

Puberty may have played a role, but looking better from the outside doesn’t tell you how she’s doing on the inside. She doesn’t need to have been mistreated by you, or to be in crisis, to benefit from support. Her dad’s experience doesn’t tell you what she needs, either. And declining a school group then isn’t inconsistent with wanting one-on-one help now.

Start with something like: **“I’m glad you told me. I know you seem to be doing better, but I don’t want to assume I know how you feel. What are you hoping therapy could help with? You don’t have to tell me everything for me to help you find someone.”**

Given her history, also ask calmly and directly whether she’s been hurting herself again, has urges to do so, or has thoughts of suicide. If she reports recent self-harm or suicidal thoughts, seek prompt professional guidance. If she has a plan or intent to act, has seriously injured herself, or can’t stay safe, stay with her and seek emergency help.

If there’s no immediate danger, **an initial appointment is a reasonable next step, not a commitment to ongoing weekly therapy.** Her pediatrician can help assess what she needs and suggest affordable options. You can also check insurance coverage, community clinics, sliding-scale providers, or whether her school offers individual counseling or referrals. If private therapy is out of reach, tell her you believe her and will work with her to find another option. The important thing is not to let “you seem fine” be the end of the conversation.

**Mild YTA for laughing at her, not for thinking £50 is steep.**

You don’t have to think the honey is worth £50. Your wife likes it enough to pay that, and part of what she values is supporting a local beekeeper. You ate the lot, so replacing it means buying the same stuff, not finding a cheaper jar and declaring it close enough. You’re already planning to do that, which is the right move.

The bit worth apologising for is telling her she got fleeced right after you polished off the evidence. “Sorry I ate it all and then took the piss out of what you paid. I’ll order you another jar.” No need to settle the fair market value of honey first.

**NTA.** You were trying to avoid awkwardness, not hurt your friend. But by pulling away without explaining, you left her wondering what she’d done. You don’t need to end a friendship to make room for a relationship she hasn’t even said she wants.

**Yes, tell her why you pulled back—but own your decision rather than passing along the office gossip.** You could say:

> “I’m sorry I went quiet. You didn’t do anything wrong. I got worried that people at work might misread how close we are, and I thought stepping back would make things less awkward. Instead, I think I made things awkward between us. I value our friendship, and I’d like to get back to talking like we used to, if you’d like that too.”

You don’t need to lead with what you heard about your coworker’s jealousy or what others think the T-shirts mean. A gift isn’t proof of romantic interest, and his interest in her doesn’t make it your job to step aside. If she asks what prompted the worry, be honest that it came from secondhand comments, not something either of them said to you directly.

If you *want* more distance for your own comfort, that’s okay. But if you miss the friendship and the only reason you backed away was to give him a chance, it’s reasonable to reconnect and let the two of them decide what they want.

**NTA for wanting to avoid awkwardness, but I’d rethink the distance.** You stepped back to spare a coworker’s feelings, but in doing so you changed a friendship your friend seems to value without giving her a say. His interest in her doesn’t make you an obstacle, and you don’t know whether she’s interested in him. The T-shirts don’t establish that she has romantic feelings for you, either.

**Yes, tell her why you pulled back—but own your decision rather than passing along office gossip.** You could say:

> “I got worried that people at work might misread how close we are, so I pulled back instead of talking to you. You didn’t do anything wrong. I’m sorry I left you wondering. I value our friendship, and I’d like to get back to talking like we used to, if you’d like that too.”

You don’t need to tell her what you heard about his jealousy or what others think the gifts mean. If she asks for more detail, be honest about what you know firsthand and what was secondhand. 

It’s fine to take space if **you** want it or if a boundary actually gets crossed. But you don’t need to give up a friendship to make a potential romance easier for someone else. Let her decide whom she wants to date, and let the two of you decide what friendship looks like.

**Mild YTA for laughing at her, not for thinking £50 is steep.**

You don’t have to think the honey is worth £50 to replace it. You polished off something she’d bought and was using a little at a time, so replacing it with the same stuff is fair. And “I wouldn’t pay that much for honey” is different from “you got fleeced.” She knew what she was paying for and valued the local producer and conservation work. You don’t have to value those things at the same price.

Buy her the jar and say, “Sorry I ate it all and took the piss out of what you paid. It was genuinely delicious.” Then get a cheaper jar for your next bread-and-butter raid.

**NTA for taking some space, but I’d talk to her rather than keep pulling away.** You were trying to avoid awkwardness, not hurt anyone. Still, from her side, a close friend suddenly became distant without telling her why. It makes sense that she asked, and it makes sense that you miss the friendship.

You’ve heard secondhand that he’s jealous, but you don’t know whether she’s interested in him. The T-shirts aren’t enough to conclude she has feelings for you, either. You don’t need to manage a possible romance by stepping out of the picture. She can decide whom she wants to date and whom she wants to be friends with.

**Tell her the truth about your decision without passing along the office gossip.** You could say:

> “I’m sorry I went quiet. I got worried our friendship might be misread at work, so I pulled back instead of talking to you. You didn’t do anything wrong. I value our friendship, and I miss talking with you.”

If you genuinely want more space, it’s okay to say so. But if the only reason you stepped back was to give him a chance, I’d reconnect. You can be considerate of his feelings without making them the basis for your friendship with her.

**A little bit YTA for the delivery, not the intent.** You meant, “Whoa, I can still smell those delicious meatballs.” She heard, “Your cooking smells like a fart.” You can see why that didn’t land as a compliment.

Since you’re already talking about it, try: “I genuinely loved your meatballs. I meant that my fart smelled like dinner, not that dinner smelled like a fart. But I get why it sounded insulting, and I’m sorry.”

Next time, “Those meatballs were incredible. Will you make them again?” gets the whole compliment across without the field report.

**NAH.** You weren’t insulting her cooking; you shared a gross observation because you found it funny and genuinely loved the meatballs. But “my fart smells like your cooking” is a pretty easy sentence to hear as “your cooking smells like a fart,” especially after you’ve just made someone dinner.

I’d go with: “Those meatballs were genuinely delicious. I meant that my fart smelled like dinner, not that dinner smelled like a fart. Sorry I made that comparison at all.”

Then let the compliment stand on its own. No need to make a case for how accurate the smell was.

You’re not the asshole for thinking £50 is steep. You were a bit of an asshole for polishing off her honey and then laughing at her for what she paid.

“More than I’d spend on honey” is a fair opinion. “You got fleeced” is a claim you haven’t really backed up. She’s paying for honey she loves and, as she understands it, supporting a local producer and bee conservation. You don’t have to value those things at £50 to respect that she does.

Buy her the same jar, as you already plan to, and give her a quick “Sorry I ate it all and took the piss out of what you paid.” Then get a cheaper jar for your next bread-and-butter raid.

**NAH.** You were sharing a weird observation, not insulting her meatballs. But “my fart smells like your cooking” is a pretty easy sentence to hear as a roast, even if you delivered it with genuine enthusiasm.

You don’t need to apologize for having IBS or passing gas. A quick apology for how the comparison landed is enough: “I meant that I recognized the smell, not that your cooking smells like farts. I loved the meatballs. Sorry—that was a gross way to say it.”

Next time, “Those meatballs were incredible” can be the whole review.

**YTA for knocking the kid over, not for evacuating.** You smelled smoke and were right to get out quickly. But calling “excuse me” doesn’t make it safe to squeeze past a child on a staircase. A fall could injure the child or block the exit for people behind you.

You also don’t know that the mom didn’t care. She may have been moving as fast as her kids could safely manage. Unless there was an immediate threat that made even a brief pause unsafe, the better move was to slow down, clearly ask for room to pass, and pass only when there was space.

If you see her again, ask if her child is okay and apologize without blaming her: “I panicked when I smelled smoke, but I shouldn’t have pushed past you. I’m sorry I knocked your kid over.”

**NTA. You were right to say something.** His apology addressed the teasing, but it didn’t address what made the comment sting: when you’re both home, you’re doing most of the hands-on care while he gets more freedom to play with the baby or take a break. You can appreciate the apology and still need a conversation about that. And from what you wrote, you didn’t reject it—you told him why you were hurt.

When you’re both calmer, I’d bring it up separately from the “mean” comment. You could say: “I appreciate that you apologized. What I still want to talk about is how we split childcare when we’re both home. I feel like I’m always the parent on duty, and I want both of us to get time to play with her and time to take a break. Can we agree on which routines each of us will handle?”

Make the agreement concrete: maybe he takes the morning shift on his days off, including feeding and diapers, while you get an uninterrupted coffee or some time to yourself. The key is that he owns the shift without you having to ask or supervise.

One separate safety note: if she’s close enough to the edge of the bed that you need to stop her from rolling, the floor is a better place to play. That doesn’t make you mean, and it doesn’t change the need for a fairer split.

**YTA for knocking over the child, not for evacuating.** The alarm and the smell of smoke gave you good reason to get out quickly. But running past a family without enough room to clear them put a child at risk of falling down the stairs and could have slowed everyone’s escape.

You don’t know that the mom “didn’t care.” She may have been moving as fast as her kids could safely go, or she may not have had room to move aside. Calling “excuse me” was reasonable; assuming they could clear your path in time wasn’t.

If you see her again, apologize without blaming her pace: “I panicked and knocked your child over. I’m sorry. Are they okay?” Next time, evacuate promptly, use the handrail, and pass only when there’s room to do so safely.

No, you weren’t wrong to say something. You can accept his apology for calling you mean and still need a conversation about why it stung. He apologized for the teasing; that didn’t address the fact that you feel like the default parent even when you’re both home.

If he was worried about the baby being near the edge, it was fair to speak up. “Let’s move her to the middle” would have been more useful than “you’re being mean.” But you don’t need to settle who was right about that moment before talking about childcare.

When you have a calm moment, make the request concrete: “I appreciate the apology. The bigger issue is that on your days off, I’m still the one who notices and handles most of what she needs. I want us both to get time to play with her and time to take a break. Can we split up the routine so I’m not always the one on duty?”

For example, he could own the morning routine on his days off—feeding, diaper changes, and keeping an eye on her—without you having to prompt him. You could also agree on a block of uninterrupted time for each of you. If he walks away again, it’s reasonable to ask, “When can we come back to this?” Taking a break from a conversation is fine; leaving the issue unresolved isn’t a workable plan.

You’re not asking him to apologize harder. You’re asking him to share the work.

You weren’t wrong to evacuate quickly. You were wrong to rush past so close that you knocked a child over on the stairs.

Smelling smoke makes the urgency understandable. But calling “excuse me” doesn’t mean there’s room to pass, and the fact that the mother didn’t move aside doesn’t mean she didn’t care. She may have been moving as fast as her kids could safely go. A fall on the stairs could seriously injure the child and make it harder for others to get out.

If you see her again, ask if her child is okay and apologize without blaming her pace: “I panicked and tried to squeeze past. I’m sorry I knocked your child over.” In a future evacuation, move promptly, but slow down enough around others to pass only when there’s room. The issue isn’t that you tried to save yourself; it’s how you passed them.

You’re not an asshole for wanting him at the cabin. But I wouldn’t use the haircut to persuade him. He already feels self-conscious, and “you wouldn’t be comfortable going” could land as “yes, it really does look that bad,” even if you mean it as giving him an out.

Tell him what you actually want him to know: “I know why you said yes, and I’m proud of you for getting the award. I said I was fine with the change, but I’m more disappointed than I let on. We hardly get time together, and the cabin was going to feel like our Christmas. I’d love for you to spend the day with us. Is there a way to do some of both?”

Maybe he can spend most of the day at the cabin and pop in for the award if the timing works. If *he* brings up skipping the event because of his hair, you can tell him you’d love to have him there without agreeing that the haircut should decide it. You can respect his choice and still be honest that the change matters to you.

No, you weren’t wrong to say something. And it sounds less like you rejected his apology and more like you explained why the comment stung. You can accept “I’m sorry I teased you” and still need a conversation about how childcare is divided. Those are two separate issues.

It’s possible he was teasing, as he said, or that he was uncomfortable with how you were playing near the edge of the bed. Moving her to the floor was a sensible call. But even if the comment was harmlessly intended, it makes sense that it landed badly when you feel like you handle most of the routine care and he gets more of the playful moments. His walking away doesn’t tell you why he didn’t respond, but it did leave that concern unresolved.

I’d bring it up again when you’re both calm, without making the joke the focus: “I appreciate that you apologized. What I still want to talk about is how we split baby care when we’re both home. I’m usually the one tracking feeds, diapers, and naps, and I want us both to get playtime and real breaks. Can we agree on some times when you’re fully on duty and some when I am?”

Start with something concrete, like him owning the morning routine on his days off or taking a regular block where he handles whatever the baby needs without you having to ask. The goal isn’t to prove it’s exactly 90 percent. It’s to make sure you’re not always the default parent when you’re both home.

**NTA for asking him to choose the cabin, but don’t make the haircut your argument.** He already feels self-conscious about it. Saying “you wouldn’t be comfortable going” puts words in his mouth and could make him wonder whether you really meant it when you told him he looked handsome.

The real issue is that you were looking forward to rare time together, and this cabin day was going to be a bit of Christmas away from home. It’s okay to admit you’re more disappointed than you let on. You could say:

> “I know I said I was fine with you going, and I understand why the award matters. But I’ve realized how much I was looking forward to having that day with you. I’d love it if you chose the cabin. If you want to accept the award in person, could we figure out whether you can do that and still spend some of the day with us?”

If *he* brings up the haircut as a reason he’d rather skip the work event, you can tell him he’s welcome at the cabin without reinforcing his worries about how he looks. His bosses have already told him what he “has” to do; you can tell him what you want without making it another obligation.

**You’re not an asshole for wanting him at the cabin.** But I wouldn’t use the haircut to make the case. He already feels self-conscious about it, and “you wouldn’t be comfortable going” makes that decision for him. If he brings up skipping the party because of his hair, it’s fine to say you’d love to have him at the cabin.

The real issue is worth saying out loud: you rarely get a day together, and this was going to be your Christmas celebration away from home. It makes sense that you’re more disappointed than you initially let on. His award matters, too, and it’s understandable that pressure from three bosses made declining awkward.

You could say: “I know I said I was fine with you going, and I do want you to enjoy being recognized. But I’ve realized I’m more disappointed than I let on. I’ve been looking forward to having a whole day with you. Could we look at the timing again and see if there’s a way to get more cabin time together?”

Maybe he can spend part of the day at the cabin and go to work just for the award, if the timing allows. If not, you can tell him you’d prefer he stick with the original plan without making either choice a test of how much he cares. **Ask for the time together, not for the haircut to decide.**

**YTA for unloading on her and calling her a name.** Being exhausted and frustrated makes sense. It doesn’t justify insulting her.

You came home after a brutal shift and drive, but she’d been parenting solo for weeks and was dealing with morning sickness. Some unfolded laundry and dirty dishes don’t tell you how much she’s been doing. And agreeing to be a stay-at-home parent didn’t mean she promised a spotless apartment or that dinner would always be her job when you’re home.

Apologize without a “but”: “I was exhausted, but calling you lazy and insulting you was wrong. I’m sorry. I came home and judged the mess without asking how you were doing.” Once you’ve both had some rest, talk about what would make your return days easier: an easy dinner, a planned nap for you, and a real break for her. If the rotation isn’t working for your family, talk about that separately rather than bringing up the move as a reason she deserved less patience.

Also, working from 3:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. and then driving 23 hours without sleep is dangerous. Build in a sleep stop or arrange another way home next time.

You weren’t wrong to be annoyed. You were sharing upsetting news and looking for comfort from friends and family, not inviting a debate about the mechanism. Even if your acquaintance meant to help, leading with a correction rather than “I’m sorry you’re dealing with that” can feel dismissive.

Snapping at her would probably make the exchange about your tone instead of why the comment bothered you. But you don’t have to apologize for being upset or tell her she was right. Cholinergic urticaria is typically triggered by a rise in body temperature, and “an allergy to bacteria on your skin” isn’t a reliable general description of it.

If you want to reply, you could say: “I was using shorthand to explain what happens when I get hot or sweat. I’m still processing the diagnosis, and I was really looking for support.” Leaving the comment unanswered is fine, too.

And reaching out to faraway friends and family is a perfectly reasonable use of Facebook. Wanting comfort after a diagnosis isn’t childish; pausing before replying was a good call.

**YTA for blowing up and calling her a name, not for feeling exhausted or wanting help.** After a long shift and a 23-hour drive, it makes sense that being handed dinner duty felt like the last straw. But a pile of clean laundry and some dirty dishes aren’t evidence that your wife is lazy. She’s been parenting solo for weeks, and now she’s dealing with morning sickness. The agreement that she’d stay home didn’t mean the house would always be caught up.

Start with an apology that doesn’t turn into a debate about the chores: “I’m sorry I called you that. I was exhausted, but that doesn’t excuse how I spoke to you.” Once you’ve both had a chance to rest, ask what the last few weeks have been like for her and tell her what you need on arrival day. You might agree on takeout that night, a chance for you to sleep, and a clear stretch of time the next day when you take over with the kids so she gets a break too. If you can afford it, occasional cleaning help might take pressure off both of you.

Whether to move is a separate conversation. It’s fair to want to live closer so you can share more of the day-to-day parenting, but “you should’ve moved” doesn’t resolve what happened here. And for your next trip, plan to stop and sleep rather than driving 23 hours straight after a full shift. That’s a serious safety risk, apart from how hard it makes that first evening home.

You’re not wrong for being annoyed. You were telling friends and family about a diagnosis that could change your day-to-day life, and you wanted comfort, not a debate about the mechanism. Facebook was a reasonable way to reach people who live far away.

A harsh snap would probably be disproportionate to one tactless comment, especially since you don’t know how she meant it. But you don’t have to pretend it landed well. Pausing before replying was a good call, and you don’t need to call yourself childish for having a reaction you chose not to act on.

You also don’t have to say she was right: a reaction to skin bacteria isn’t the standard explanation for cholinergic urticaria. You can skip the medical debate and say, “I was using shorthand for what happens when I get hot or sweat. I’m still processing the diagnosis, and I was really just looking for some support.” Or you can leave the comment unanswered.

NTA for getting angry. You didn’t do anything wrong by falling asleep at a party. Putting makeup on you and writing sexual comments on you while you were asleep crossed a boundary. It doesn’t matter whether they meant it as a joke or thought the comments were flattering.

Did you lose your temper? It sounds like you did, at least in the ordinary sense that you were furious and called them horrible people. That’s a judgment about who they are, rather than what they did, but you don’t have to defend every word you said to know your anger was justified.

You don’t owe them dinner or a reply. If you want to respond, you could say: “I appreciate the apology, but I’m not interested in dinner. What you did wasn’t okay, and I’d prefer you not contact me again.” If you’re considering reporting it, you can make that decision separately from whether you accept their apology.

Yes—you were in the wrong for unloading on your wife and calling her a name. You weren’t wrong to feel frustrated: you came home exhausted, saw chores piling up, and were asked to make dinner when you badly needed sleep. But dishes and a pile of clean laundry don’t show that she’s lazy or that she hasn’t been pulling her weight. She’s been parenting two kids while you’re away for weeks at a time, and now she’s dealing with morning sickness.

Start with an apology that doesn’t turn into a debate about the house: “I’m sorry I called you that and took my frustration out on you. I was exhausted, but that doesn’t excuse it.” Later, when you’ve both had a chance to talk, ask how she’s been managing and explain what you need on arrival days. You might agree that you get a block of sleep when you first get home, then take over dinner or kid duty so she gets a break too.

Moving closer to work can be a separate conversation. It might let you help more, but it’s a joint decision, not a reason she deserved what you said. In the meantime, it’s worth revisiting the agreement you made before she was pregnant and figuring out what’s realistic now.

One other thing: a 23-hour drive immediately after a full shift is dangerous for you and everyone else on the road. Next time, sleep before leaving or break up the trip.

You’re not wrong to be irritated. You were sharing upsetting health news with friends and family because you wanted support, and getting a technical correction instead can feel dismissive—even if she didn’t mean it that way. Using a private Facebook post to reach loved ones who live far away is a reasonable way to ask for comfort.

Snapping at her to unload some of your anger would be unfair, but telling her how the comment landed isn’t the same as snapping. You also don’t have to concede that she was right: cholinergic urticaria can be triggered by a rise in body temperature, often when you sweat, but it isn’t generally described as an allergy to skin bacteria.

If you still want to respond, you could say: “I was using shorthand to explain the diagnosis. I’m still processing it, and I was looking for support more than a discussion of the terminology.” It’s also fine to leave the comment unanswered and reach out directly to someone you trust for the support you were hoping for.

You caught the impulse before acting on it. That’s good judgment, not something to beat yourself up over.

No, you weren’t wrong to get angry. Falling asleep at a party isn’t consent to have people put makeup on you or write sexual remarks on your body. It doesn’t matter whether they meant it as a joke or a compliment.

Calling them “horrible people” sounds like you spoke in anger. If you regret that wording, you can walk it back without taking back the point: **what they did was unacceptable**. Telling them you might report it wasn’t inherently an overreaction, either.

Their apology may be sincere, but you don’t owe them dinner, forgiveness, or even a reply. If you want to respond, you could say: “I appreciate the apology, but I don’t want to meet. What you did crossed a line. How did you get my number?” Or, if you’d rather not hear from them again, you can simply ask them not to contact you.

**NTA for getting angry.** Putting makeup on you and writing sexual remarks on you while you were asleep crossed a boundary. Falling asleep at a party didn’t give anyone permission, and the fact that the remarks were meant as compliments doesn’t change that.

Calling them “horrible people” was harsh. If that’s the part you regret, you can acknowledge it without backing down: “I shouldn’t have called you horrible people, but what you did was not okay.” You don’t have to apologize for being angry.

You don’t owe them dinner or even a reply. If you’d rather respond, you could say: “I appreciate the apology, but I don’t want to meet. Please don’t contact me again.” Whether to report it is a separate decision: think about what you want from reporting it and who’s in a position to help, such as the host or organizer. Their apology doesn’t obligate you to drop it.

**YTA.** You’re right that handling pressure is part of being president. The problem is that you weren’t trying to give Sam a fair chance to show he could handle it. You were trying to make him fail so you could win.

His struggle wasn’t meaningless, but it showed that he struggled during that particular trial. It didn’t prove he couldn’t grow into the role with a proper handoff, and it didn’t prove you’d do better. You didn’t have to pass the same test. Winning after he lost support tells you the tactic worked, not that it helped the team.

A fairer approach would’ve been to propose a trial with clear expectations, support, and the same opportunity for every candidate—including you. If you want to make things right with Sam, own the part you controlled: “I pushed for that trial because I wanted to hurt your chances. That was unfair, and I’m sorry.” You don’t have to pretend he handled the job well to acknowledge that you treated him badly.

You’re not an asshole for feeling uneasy around X, but I think you overstepped when that discomfort turned into your girlfriend cutting him off.

Given your history with X and the fact that he’d led her on before, it makes sense that you’d be wary of him. But standing close together at band practice doesn’t, on its own, mean either of them crossed a line. “Don’t get too close” was vague, and the fix isn’t to give her a more precise rule about how close she can stand. It’s to talk about what you both consider flirting or disrespect, and trust her to decide how to respond if he does cross a line.

It’s also fair to be bothered that she said she’d blocked him when she hadn’t. You can address that without making blocking him the test of whether she’s honest or loyal. She should be able to say, “I don’t want to block him,” even if that’s not what you want to hear.

You could say: “I’m sorry I put pressure on you to stop talking to X. I still don’t trust him, but I don’t want to decide who you can be friends with. I was hurt when you said you’d blocked him and hadn’t. I’d rather you tell me what you actually want, even if we disagree. What do you want to do?”

Then give her room to answer. If she wants distance from him, respect that; if she wants to stay friends, don’t treat that choice by itself as a betrayal.

You’re not an asshole for feeling uneasy about X, but you overstepped when that discomfort turned into pressure for your girlfriend to stop talking to him. Given his history with both of you, it makes sense that you don’t trust him. But trusting your girlfriend means trusting her to decide how to respond if he crosses a line. Standing close at band practice, by itself, doesn’t show that either of them did anything wrong.

It’s fair to be bothered that she said she’d blocked him when she hadn’t. She should be able to tell you honestly that she doesn’t want to block someone, and you should be able to hear that without treating it as disloyalty. The lesson isn’t that you should’ve spelled out exactly how close they could be. It’s that “don’t be too close” was vague and put her in the position of trying to guess what would upset you.

You could say: “I’m sorry I pushed you to cut X off. I still don’t trust him, but I don’t want to decide who you can talk to. I was hurt when you said you’d blocked him and hadn’t, and I’d rather we be honest when we disagree. What do *you* want your friendship with him to look like?”

Then give her room to answer, even if it’s not the answer you’d prefer. If your concern is flirting, talk about what both of you consider flirting and how you’d each handle it. That’s a more useful agreement than policing who she talks to or how close they stand.

**YTA.** You weren’t wrong to think the team should care about leadership skills, not just popularity. You were wrong to arrange a test for a rival because you wanted him to fail, then treat that failure as proof you deserved the job.

Sam’s trial showed that he struggled with the work under those conditions. That’s relevant, but it doesn’t tell you how he would have done with a normal handoff, time to learn, or support from the team. And unless you took the same test under the same conditions, it tells you nothing about whether you would have handled it better. The captain’s agreement makes her part of the decision; it doesn’t take you off the hook.

The simplest fairness check: would you have agreed to the same trial for yourself, with the same stakes, if Sam had proposed it? A transparent trial offered to all candidates could have helped the team make an informed choice. Singling out your strongest rival helped *you*, and winning the election doesn’t prove those were the same thing.

If you want to make it right, apologize without relitigating whether he’d have been a good president: “I pushed for that trial because I wanted to improve my chances of winning. It wasn’t fair to put you under scrutiny I wasn’t willing to put myself under. I’m sorry.”

You’re not an asshole for feeling uneasy about X. Given what you know about how he treated your girlfriend before you dated, your distrust is understandable. But I think you handled that unease unfairly when a vague agreement about not being “too close” turned into her blocking him and not speaking to him at band. Standing close together isn’t, by itself, evidence of flirting or of either of them crossing a clear line.

It’s also fair to be bothered that she said she blocked him when she hadn’t. You can ask for honesty without insisting on the block: “I’d rather you tell me you disagree with me than say you did something you didn’t.” She said she wanted to avoid problems with X; that helps explain her hesitation, but it doesn’t make the mismatch unimportant.

The repair isn’t to give her a more precise rule about how close she can stand to him. It’s to talk about what each of you considers appropriate behavior with friends and what you’d do if someone actually flirted or pushed a boundary. You might say:

> “I’m sorry I turned my distrust of X into pressure on you to stop talking to him. I don’t want you to keep him blocked just to avoid a fight with me. I do want us to be honest when we disagree. What do *you* want your friendship with him to look like?”

Then give her room to answer, including if she wants to stay friends or keep her distance. You don’t have to trust X to trust your girlfriend to decide how she’ll respond to him.

YTA for setting up a test to make a rival fail, not for thinking candidates should demonstrate they can do the job.

You’re right that paperwork, conflict, and pressure are relevant to whether someone is ready to lead. Sam struggling enough that the president had to step in is evidence that he wasn’t ready to handle those duties **under those conditions**. It doesn’t prove he would have been a terrible president after a normal handover, and it says nothing about how you would have performed under the same test. Winning after he lost support isn’t proof that the team got the better leader.

The unfair part is that you singled Sam out for a high-stakes trial because you expected his failure to help you win. The president’s ability to step in protected the team from some of the fallout, but it didn’t make the selection process fair. If readiness was the concern, you could have proposed the same trial for all candidates, including yourself, with clear expectations and comparable support.

If you want to make it right, you can apologize without pretending his performance was fine: “I pushed for that trial because I wanted to win. It wasn’t fair to put you under a spotlight I wasn’t willing to put myself under. I’m sorry.”

**Mild YTA if you counted on their help without getting a clear yes on this specific deal.** Not for buying used—that was a reasonable choice. And you didn’t actually spend their money: you made the down payment yourselves, and they haven’t contributed to the monthly payments yet.

The key question is what they agreed to on those calls. Keeping them updated isn’t the same as hearing, “Yes, we’ll still help with the payments on this used car after you put money down.” You and your wife saw it as meeting in the middle, but a compromise needs both sides to agree. On the other hand, if they explicitly approved those terms before you signed and only objected afterward, then it’s fair to feel they moved the goalposts.

Looking at only two cars doesn’t automatically mean you made a bad purchase. But wanting to get the shopping over with wasn’t a good reason to leave the funding question unresolved. I’d have you and your wife say, “We appreciated the offer. We thought you were okay with the plan based on our calls, but we should have confirmed before signing. Can you tell us what, if anything, you’re still comfortable contributing?” Then budget as though the payments are yours unless they clearly commit. You get to choose the car; they get to choose whether to help pay for it.

**Mild YTA if you bought the car counting on their help without getting a clear yes.** Not because you chose a used car—that may have been the better financial decision—but because you and your wife decided what counted as a compromise without confirming that her parents agreed to fund it.

Your edit matters: you weren’t hiding the purchase, and if they knew the specific car and financing terms and explicitly said they’d still help, it would be unfair for them to back out just because they disliked the final choice. But keeping them updated isn’t the same as getting their agreement. The key question before signing was: “We’re buying this used car and putting this much down. Are you still willing to help with the monthly payments?”

Looking at only two cars doesn’t automatically mean you made a bad purchase. But wanting to be done shopping was a reason to slow down long enough to settle who was paying, not a reason to assume the offer still stood.

I’d have your wife and you say something like: “We appreciate the offer. We thought we were keeping you in the loop, but we should have asked directly whether you’d still help with this car. We don’t want you to feel obligated because we already signed.” Then budget as though the payments are yours unless they clearly recommit. You get to choose the car; they get to choose whether to contribute.

You’re not an asshole for accidentally knocking her phone off the bed. But if it worked before the fall and wouldn’t turn on afterward, an apology alone was probably not enough. It’s fair that she was upset.

Her previous drops and screen repairs matter when figuring out what the phone was worth, but they don’t erase your part in what happened. And the $30 she paid a friend isn’t necessarily what it would cost to get another phone in similar condition. You don’t owe her a brand-new iPhone, but it’s reasonable to offer to get a repair estimate and cover a reasonable repair or comparable used replacement.

You can still bring it up: “I’m sorry I knocked your phone down. I should’ve offered to help make it right. Can we find out what it would cost to fix it?”

You can take responsibility for the accident without taking responsibility for every bit of damage the phone already had.

**Soft YTA if you bought the car expecting them to help with the payments without confirming they’d contribute to this specific purchase.** Not because you bought used—that can be a sensible choice—but because your compromise wasn’t necessarily one they agreed to.

Your edit matters: you didn’t hide the purchase from them. But there’s a difference between keeping them updated and hearing, “Yes, we’ll help with the monthly payments on this used car, with this down payment.” If they said that before you signed and then backed out, your frustration is justified. If they were still objecting, or never clearly agreed, it wasn’t fair to treat their general offer as a commitment. You and your wife get to choose the car; they get to decide whether to subsidize it.

Looking at only two cars doesn’t automatically mean you made a bad purchase. The bigger issue is whether you can afford the loan without their help. You haven’t spent their money, and they aren’t locked in—you’re the ones who signed.

I’d start with: “We thought keeping you updated meant we were on the same page, but we should’ve confirmed before signing. Are you still comfortable helping with this car? If so, how much and for how long?” Until you have a clear answer, budget as though the payments are entirely yours.

**NTA for feeling hurt or wanting more attention from your husband.** But asking him to stop texting a longtime friend altogether may not be the fairest first step. Daily texting can feel like a lot, especially if you’re struggling to stay connected while he’s on the rig, but the frequency alone doesn’t tell you whether anything inappropriate is happening. Her being single doesn’t tell you that either.

I’d revisit the conversation when you’re both calm and get specific about what’s hurting. Is he texting her during your limited time together? Do you rarely hear from him when he’s away? Or is there secrecy or flirtation that makes this feel different from an ordinary friendship? Those are different problems, and they call for different boundaries.

You could say: “I know she’s a longtime friend. When I see you two texting throughout the day and I feel like we barely get time to connect, I feel sidelined. Can we talk about how to make more time for us, both when you’re home and when you’re on the rig?”

A regular check-in while he’s away or phone-free time together when he’s home might address what you actually need. If there’s secrecy or flirtation, name that directly rather than debating how many texts are too many. Being his priority doesn’t mean getting all his attention; it does mean he takes your concerns seriously and makes consistent time for your marriage.

You’re not an asshole for an accident, but if the phone worked before you knocked it off the bed and stopped working right after, it’s fair to do more than apologize.

Her past drops matter when figuring out what the phone was worth, not whether you should offer to help. You don’t owe her a brand-new iPhone, and the $30 she paid a friend isn’t necessarily what it costs to replace it. Offer to help get a repair estimate. If fixing it costs more than a comparable used phone in similar condition, use that replacement cost as a starting point.

You could say: “I’m sorry I knocked your phone off the bed. I should’ve offered to help when it wouldn’t turn on. Can we see what it would cost to fix it and figure out what’s fair?”

You’re not an asshole for feeling hurt or wanting more attention from your husband. But asking him to stop texting a longtime friend altogether may be premature. Texting most days isn’t proof that anything inappropriate is happening, and her being single isn’t the issue. What matters is whether their contact is crowding out your time together or crossing a boundary in your marriage.

I’d revisit the conversation when you’re both calm and get specific about what you need. For example:

> “I’m not asking you to give up your friendship. I’ve been feeling disconnected from you, and seeing how often you two text makes that feeling stronger. I’d like us to have more time and attention for each other. Can we talk about what that would look like, both when you’re home and when you’re on the rig?”

If what you miss is uninterrupted time together, ask for phone-free dinners or evenings. If it’s connection while he’s away, ask for a regular check-in that works with his shifts. If there’s something about the messages themselves that bothers you—flirting, secrecy, or sharing private details about your marriage—name that directly rather than making it about her personality.

Being his priority doesn’t mean you have to get every text or that he can’t be close to friends. It does mean you should be able to raise a concern and have him take it seriously. I’d pay more attention to whether he listens and follows through on changes you agree to than to the raw number of texts.

You’re not wrong for wanting to feel like a priority in your marriage. Texting a friend throughout the day, nearly every day, is worth talking about if you’re feeling less connected to him. But the frequency alone doesn’t tell you whether the friendship is inappropriate, and her being single doesn’t make it so. Being his priority doesn’t mean he can’t give attention to friends; it does mean your relationship needs time and care.

I’d start by asking for what you need rather than asking him to cut her off. You could say: “I’ve noticed you two text throughout the day, and I’ve been feeling disconnected from you. I miss hearing from you when you’re away and having time together when you’re home. Can we talk about what this friendship is like for you and agree on some time that’s just for us?”

Then get specific. Maybe it’s a regular check-in while he’s on the rig, if his schedule allows, or phone-free time together at home. If what’s bothering you is flirting, secrecy, or him repeatedly interrupting your time together to respond to her, name that behavior directly. Those are different concerns from how often two friends text.

What I’d pay most attention to is how he responds: he doesn’t have to agree to stop texting her to take you seriously, but he should be willing to hear what’s hurting and work with you on it.

You’re not a jerk for an accident, but I think stopping at an apology fell short. Her phone was working before it hit the floor and wouldn’t turn on afterward. That makes your drop the likely trigger, even if earlier damage made it more fragile.

Her history with the phone matters when figuring out what’s fair to pay, not whether to offer help. You don’t owe her a brand-new iPhone, but the $30 she paid a friend isn’t necessarily what it costs to replace it with a similar used phone. I’d offer to cover a diagnostic and then discuss a reasonable repair or comparable used replacement, taking its prior condition into account.

You could say: “I’ve been thinking about your phone. I’m sorry I dropped it, and I should’ve offered to help when it stopped turning on. Can we find out what it would cost to fix and figure out what’s fair?”

**A mild YTA for how you left, not for refusing to drive an extra hour while exhausted.** Since you drove B to the party knowing she planned to drink, it was reasonable for her to expect a ride back unless you’d agreed otherwise. You could change the plan, but waking her up to say you were leaving isn’t the same as making sure she had a safe alternative.

The bigger concern is what you mean by “passed out.” If she woke easily, could respond coherently, and a sober host agreed to stay with her, leaving her there could have been fine. If she was hard to wake, couldn’t stay awake, or was breathing slowly or irregularly, that’s a reason to call emergency services and stay with her, not arrange a ride. I’m glad she found another way home, but you didn’t know that would happen when you left.

Your boyfriend also bears responsibility: he encouraged the drinking challenge, and it shouldn’t have fallen solely on you to deal with the aftermath. Next time, agree on rides before anyone starts drinking. And if you’re too tired to drive safely, don’t drive—make sure there’s a sober handoff instead.

**YTA in that moment.** Not because you necessarily made anything up, but because you publicly aired their dad’s conduct at an assembly meant to help two classmates who’d just lost their home. They didn’t start the fire, and the fundraiser was for them.

The school calling it a rumour probably felt unfair when you’d been there. But seeing the grow setup and hearing their dad admit to it isn’t the same as knowing exactly what started the fire. And even if you were right about the cause, shouting it out in front of the whole school didn’t help the girls. If you thought the school was misleading people, you could’ve raised it privately with a teacher.

You were 16, and this was a long time ago. You don’t need to beat yourself up over it. The useful takeaway is that you can be right about what you saw and still be wrong about when and how you share it. And I’d leave the speculation about what their dad is doing now alone.

**A bit, yes—but not because you refused to drive an extra hour at 2 a.m.** If you were too tired to drive safely, you were right not to make the trip. The problem was leaving without first making sure someone sober was looking after B. You’d driven her there knowing she’d be drinking, so unless you’d agreed otherwise, it was reasonable for her to expect a ride back or at least help making another plan.

More importantly, after that much liquor, being passed out is a potential medical issue, not just a transportation problem. Waking her long enough to say goodbye doesn’t necessarily mean she’s okay. If someone is hard to wake, can’t stay awake, or is breathing slowly or irregularly, call emergency services, put them on their side, and stay with them. If she was alert and a sober host had agreed to keep an eye on her, leaving would have been much more reasonable.

Your boyfriend also deserves some scrutiny: he helped turn drinking into a tolerance test, and her being annoying doesn’t make that less reckless. I’m glad she found another way home. If you want to clear the air, you can own the part that matters: “I was too tired to drive you home safely, but I should’ve made sure you were okay and had someone with you before I left.”

**Not wanting to make an hour-long detour at 2 a.m. was reasonable. Leaving without making sure B was safe is the part I’d fault.**

Since you drove her to the party knowing she’d be drinking, it was reasonable for her to expect some help getting home, even if you didn’t explicitly promise a return ride. That didn’t have to mean driving her yourself, especially if you were too tired to drive safely. If she was alert and medically okay, you could’ve helped arrange a sober ride or checked that the host was willing to let her stay.

The bigger concern is that she’d passed out after heavy drinking. I’m glad she found another way home, but that doesn’t tell us how she was doing when you left. If someone is hard to wake, can’t stay awake, or is breathing slowly or irregularly after drinking, call emergency services, put them on their side, and stay with them. A ride home isn’t the priority then.

Your boyfriend also shares responsibility: he helped turn drinking into a tolerance test, and he could’ve helped make sure B was safe afterward. Next time, agree on the ride home before anyone starts drinking, and skip the drinking challenges.

Yes, YTA for yelling it out at assembly. The issue isn’t that you made up what you saw. It’s that you publicly tied two classmates to their dad’s conduct while the school was trying to help them after a fire. They didn’t cause it, and they could have lost belongings and needed support regardless of what their dad did or what insurance eventually paid.

I can see why being told you were “starting rumours” felt unfair when you’d actually been there. But seeing the grow setup and hearing their dad confess to growing cannabis isn’t the same as knowing what ignited the fire. “Faulty appliances” could be consistent with equipment in the room, but it doesn’t establish that link or show the school was covering anything up. And growing cannabis then isn’t evidence that he was dealing or that he’s growing it now.

If you genuinely thought the school was misleading people, raising it privately with a teacher would’ve let you explain what you saw without putting the girls on the spot. You were a teenager and made an impulsive call; you can own that without making it a verdict on who you are now.

**YTA for yelling it out at assembly, not for questioning what the school said.** You had firsthand knowledge that there was a grow setup in the house. That doesn’t necessarily mean you knew it caused the fire, and “faulty appliances” could be consistent with equipment in that setup. The school calling it a rumour doesn’t mean you made up what you saw, but you stated your inference as a fact.

The bigger issue is that the fundraiser was for two girls who’d lost their home, not a referendum on their dad. They didn’t cause the fire, and announcing his arrest and alleged role in front of their peers put the embarrassment on them. If you thought the school was misleading people, you could have raised it privately with a teacher or your brigade supervisor.

You were 16, and it makes sense that being told you were spreading rumours when you’d actually been there rubbed you the wrong way. But you can stand by what you witnessed and still own that the public callout was unfair. And the suspicion about what he’s doing now is just that—leave it out.

A little, yes—for the joke, not for thinking the play was rough. There’s a difference between “some actors seemed under-rehearsed” and “they only got in because they know someone, so they don’t even try.” The first is about what you saw; the second assumes something about their effort and why they’re there. Since your friend is part of the group and has a close friend in it, it’s understandable that he heard himself included.

It also makes sense that you thought the joke would land, given how often he pokes fun at the group. But venting to a close friend and hearing that same criticism become a group joke right after a performance can feel very different. A public performance is fair to critique; that doesn’t make every setting or delivery equally considerate.

I’d apologize without debating whether he’s being hypocritical or guessing whether his crush had anything to do with it. You could say: “I wasn’t taking a dig at you. I thought you were genuinely good. But I made a sweeping joke about your group in front of everyone, and I can see why it sounded like I meant you too. I’m sorry.”

You don’t have to pretend you liked the whole play. Just own the part where you turned a fair observation about the performance into an unfair assumption about the people.

**A little, yes—for the joke, not for thinking the play was rough.** A public performance is fair to critique. But “some actors seemed underprepared” is about what you saw; “they got in through friends and family, so they don’t even try” is a claim about people’s motives. Said in front of classmates, it’s easy to see why your friend heard it as a dig at the whole group, including him.

It’s understandable that his own jokes made you think this was fair game. Still, venting to a close friend about a group you’re part of can feel different from hearing that friend mock the group in front of others. You don’t need to figure out whether the guy he likes being there made it worse; your friend already told you what bothered him.

I’d say something like: “I’m sorry I made that joke in front of everyone. I thought you did a really good job, and it wasn’t a dig at you. But I can see why it sounded that way, and it wasn’t fair of me to say people weren’t even trying.”

You don’t have to pretend you liked the whole play. Just own the difference between criticizing the performance and taking a swipe at the people in it.

You were right to object to being grabbed and pushed. Yelling at her in front of everyone wasn’t the best way to handle it, but you can apologize for yelling without backing down about the physical contact.

Her request to move the dog grooming away from the food was reasonable. Grabbing you to move you wasn’t. It sounds like you were still upset about that when she criticized how you feed your dog, so everyone at dinner heard the outburst without understanding what had led up to it.

Talk to your parents privately and tell them exactly what happened, especially since she denied pushing you. If you feel comfortable speaking to her directly, keep it simple: “I’m sorry I yelled at dinner. I should have spoken to you earlier. When you grabbed me and moved me, I felt disrespected. Next time, please ask me to move without touching me.”

Your sister is right that you could have handled it differently. That doesn’t mean you have to brush off what happened.

**NTA for being upset, but yelling wasn’t the best way to handle it.** Your housekeeper had a reasonable point about brushing the dog near dinner, but she could have asked you to move without grabbing or pushing you. It makes sense that you were still upset when she started commenting on how much you feed your dog. To everyone else at dinner, though, the outburst probably looked like it came out of nowhere.

Your sister can be right that a private conversation would have gone better without “that’s just how she is” being a reason to let it go. Tell your parents privately what happened, in concrete terms, since they didn’t see it and she denied it. Then, if you’re comfortable speaking with her directly, you could say:

> “I’m sorry I yelled at you at dinner. Earlier, when you grabbed me and moved me, I felt shocked. If I’m in the way or doing something too close to the food, please ask me to move. Don’t move me yourself.”

You can apologize for raising your voice without apologizing for the boundary.

A little, yes—but not for thinking the play was rough or saying so. The part that crossed the line was joking in front of classmates that people in the group got in through connections and therefore “don’t even try.” Missed lines and awkward silences are things you noticed; how much the actors cared or tried is something you don’t know. And since your friend’s best friend is in the group, it’s understandable that he heard the joke as including him, even though you meant the opposite.

It’s also understandable that you thought he’d laugh, given that he makes similar jokes himself. But venting to a close friend about your own group and hearing someone else mock it in front of classmates can feel different. You don’t need to figure out whether the guy he likes being there made it worse; your friend already told you what embarrassed him.

I’d apologize privately for the joke, without taking back your honest opinion of the play: “I’m sorry I joked that people in the group don’t try. That was unfair, and I can see why it sounded like I meant you too. I genuinely thought you were good. I should’ve stuck to what I noticed instead of making it personal.”

A public performance is fair to critique. “Some scenes felt under-rehearsed” is criticism of the play; “they don’t even try” is a dig at the people in it.

You weren’t wrong to be upset or to set a boundary. **The part I’d apologize for is yelling at her in front of everyone—not objecting to being grabbed and pushed.**

Her request to move the dog grooming away from the food was reasonable. If she grabbed and pushed you as you describe, that wasn’t an appropriate way to get you to move. It makes sense that the later comment about your dog hit a nerve when you hadn’t addressed what happened earlier. But because everyone else heard you yell about feeding the dog, they may not have understood what you were actually upset about.

You can apologize without taking back your account: “I’m sorry I yelled at you at dinner. I should’ve spoken to you privately. Earlier, when you grabbed me and moved me, I felt startled and upset. If you need me to move, please ask me without putting your hands on me.”

Since she denied pushing you, it’s also worth telling your mom privately exactly what you experienced, including that the request to move was fair but the physical contact wasn’t. Your sister can be right that you could’ve handled it differently without being right that you should just accept it.

**ESH.** If you weren’t staring, it was unfair of her to call you out in front of her friends. You had every right to say, “No, I was looking at the posters.” But mocking her chest and then laughing at her was cruel. Being embarrassed explains why you snapped; it doesn’t make the comeback fair.

You can apologize for your part without admitting to something you didn’t do. If there’s a natural moment when she isn’t put on the spot, keep it brief: “I wasn’t staring, but I shouldn’t have made a comment about your body or laughed. I’m sorry.” Then give her space. She doesn’t owe you a response or an apology in return.

The part worth paying attention to is that you say you go straight for insults when you feel disrespected. Next time, correct what was said without attacking the person: “I wasn’t looking at you. Please don’t tell people I was.” That’s standing up for yourself, not letting it slide.

**ESH, based on your account.** She shouldn’t have loudly accused you of staring, and you were entitled to say you weren’t. But mocking her chest and then laughing at her wasn’t defending yourself. It was humiliating her back.

You don’t have to accept a false accusation to apologize for what you actually did. Even months later, if there’s a natural moment when she isn’t on the spot, you could say: “I wasn’t staring, but what I said about your body was mean. I’m sorry I said it and laughed.” Keep it brief, don’t ask for an apology in return, and give her space.

The bigger thing to work on is the reflex you described: when you feel disrespected, you go straight for whatever will hurt most. Next time, “No, I was looking at the posters. Don’t put words in my mouth,” is enough. Her looks aren’t evidence one way or the other, and you don’t need to insult someone to stand up for yourself.

**Yes, for the comeback—not for defending yourself.** If you weren’t staring, it was unfair and embarrassing for her to announce that you were in front of other people. It makes sense that you wanted to shut it down. But “I wasn’t looking at you” would have defended you. Mocking her chest and laughing at her humiliated her without doing anything to clear up what happened.

Her appearance isn’t evidence that she was lying or that she knew you weren’t looking. She might have misread where you were looking, or she might have been trying to embarrass you. You don’t have to settle which it was to take responsibility for what you said. Your friends can be right that she started it and wrong that she deserved the response.

If there’s a natural chance to speak without an audience, you could say, “I wasn’t staring, but I shouldn’t have made that comment about your body or laughed. I’m sorry.” That’s not admitting to staring. If she seems to want space, don’t corner her or push for a response.

Since you’ve noticed this is a pattern when you feel disrespected, have a line ready for next time: “No, I wasn’t staring. Don’t tell people I was.” You can stand up for yourself without giving the other person a new reason to be hurt.

You were wrong to threaten to share your sister’s secrets and hide her charger, but that’s not the biggest issue here. An adult in your home said he would have beaten you if your mom hadn’t been there. **That’s a threat of violence, and you don’t have to wait for him to act on it before asking for help.**

It makes sense that you felt hurt when your sister sided with the adults. But she’s 11, and taking your anger out on her didn’t address what her mom’s boyfriend said. You can apologize for your part without agreeing with her: “I was hurt, but I shouldn’t have threatened to text your friends or hidden your charger. I won’t share what you told me.”

**Please tell a trusted adult outside the house as soon as you can**—your color guard coach, a school counselor, a teacher, or a relative you trust. Use his exact words and tell them that there often isn’t enough food at home. You could say: “My mom’s boyfriend said, ‘If her mom wasn’t there I would have beat the shit out of her.’ I need help figuring out what to do, and we often don’t have enough food at home.” If your phone data is off, you can tell someone in person at school. If you think he’s about to hurt you, get to a safe adult or neighbor if you can and call emergency services.

You can take responsibility for how you treated your sister without taking responsibility for an adult threatening you. A joke about a cat didn’t justify that, and paying for color guard doesn’t change what you deserve: enough food and a safe place to live.
