You were wrong to threaten to tell your sister’s friends what she’d said and to hide her charger. But that doesn’t make you the main problem here. Your sister is 11, and even though it hurt that she sided with the adults, taking it out on her didn’t address what your mom’s boyfriend said.

An adult saying he would have beaten you if your mom hadn’t been there is serious. You don’t have to wait for him to hit you to ask for help. And regularly not having enough food at home is something you deserve help with, too.

**Tell a trusted adult outside your household as soon as you can**—your color guard coach, a school counselor, a teacher, or a relative you trust. You can keep it simple: “My mom’s boyfriend said that if my mom wasn’t there, he would have beaten me. We also regularly don’t have enough food at home. I need help figuring out what to do.” If you’re worried things could get worse at home after you tell, say that up front so they can help you plan for your safety. If you think he’s about to hurt you, get to a safe place if you can and call emergency services.

Tess was out of line calling you a jerk, but her disappointment is understandable. They can know you hate weddings and still hope you’ll come because it’s theirs. If you decide not to go, I’d skip the gesture of handing back the envelope. A warm, clear conversation is less likely to feel like you’re rejecting them along with the invitation:

> “I love you both, and I’m really happy for you. I know it means a lot that you asked me, and I’m sorry I came across as dismissive. Weddings are harder for me than I’ve explained. I can’t be best man, and I’ve decided not to attend. I know that’s disappointing. I’d love to celebrate with you separately if you’re up for it.”

Before tomorrow, ask yourself one thing: **If there were no best-man duties and you could leave after the ceremony, would you want to be there?** If yes, offer that. If no, give them a kind, definite answer rather than a reluctant promise.

**NAH.** You can be proud of him for taking on a demanding job and still miss him. Telling him to nap was considerate; feeling disappointed when he slept through most of the evening doesn’t undo that. He wasn’t wrong for needing sleep, and you weren’t wrong for wanting comfort.

Your update sounds like a constructive conversation. You didn’t ask him to work less or push through exhaustion. You told him what you were missing, and together you found a way for him to recharge and for both of you to have time to connect. If he’s too tired for FaceTime some nights, a quick goodnight text or voice note could be a low-pressure fallback, if that works for both of you.

And “my mental health isn’t his responsibility” doesn’t mean “I shouldn’t ask him for support.” It’s okay to lean on your boyfriend sometimes while also having other people or routines to turn to when he’s unavailable. You don’t have to make yourself need nothing to be a supportive partner.

**NAH.** You’re not wrong for feeling hurt or frustrated when you miss him, and he’s not wrong for needing sleep after an 11-hour shift. You can know he didn’t do anything wrong and still feel disappointed that you couldn’t talk.

Your update sounds like you handled it well. You told him what was hard without asking him to change jobs or push through exhaustion. Giving him time to recharge and having a more predictable time to connect addresses something you were missing without necessarily asking for more time.

One thing I wouldn’t take from this is that because your mental health isn’t his responsibility, you shouldn’t ask him for support. It’s okay to say, “I’m having a rough day. Do you have ten minutes to talk?” It’s also okay for him to say he’s too wiped out. Having someone else you can reach out to on those nights can help without making his support any less meaningful.

Try the new routine and see how it feels for both of you. If evening calls keep getting swallowed by sleep, a short voice note or a planned weekend call might be more reliable. You don’t have to prove you support him by pretending the adjustment isn’t hard for you, too.

**NAH.** You can be disappointed that you didn’t get to talk when you were having a rough day without believing he did anything wrong by sleeping. You noticed how tired he was and encouraged him to rest. Feeling upset afterward doesn’t undo that kindness.

Your update sounds like a good conversation: you told him you missed connecting without blaming him for his hours, and you found a plan that gives him time to recharge and gives you both something to look forward to. If he’s too wiped out for FaceTime some nights, you could agree on a quick goodnight text or voice note as a fallback, so neither of you is left guessing.

And “my mental health isn’t his responsibility” doesn’t have to mean “I shouldn’t ask him for support.” It’s reasonable to want comfort from your boyfriend. It also helps to have someone else you can reach out to on a hard night when he’s asleep. You don’t have to hide your needs to be supportive of him.

**A mild YTA for treating the rehearsal dinner as a theme to dress up for, not simply for wearing a cheongsam.**

A cheongsam can be appropriate formalwear, and the bride’s mother may have genuinely liked yours. But the invitation said “cocktail formal,” and knowing that the bride and some of her relatives would wear traditional clothing wasn’t the same as being invited to match them. The “Asian” hair and makeup is the part I’d rethink most: there’s a difference between choosing a style you admire and trying to look like an ethnicity, especially if the makeup was meant to imitate facial features.

The stares don’t tell you what anyone thought, and neither your cousin’s criticism nor the bride’s mother’s compliment speaks for everyone. Since your cousin raised it, a brief acknowledgment is enough: “I meant it as appreciation, but I realize I made an assumption about what was appropriate. I’m sorry I didn’t check first.” Then follow the wedding dress code and let it go.

**A mild YTA.** Wearing a cheongsam as a non-Chinese guest isn’t inherently disrespectful. The misstep was treating the couple’s cultural celebration as a dress-up theme when the invitation just said “cocktail formal.” Knowing the bride and some relatives planned to wear cheongsams wasn’t the same as being invited to join them.

The makeup is a separate issue. If “in an Asian manner” means you copied a hairstyle or makeup look you liked, that’s one thing. If it means you tried to make your features look East Asian, that’s more likely to come across as caricature.

The bride’s mother’s compliment may have been entirely sincere, and the stares don’t tell you what anyone thought. You don’t need to turn this into a big incident. A brief acknowledgment to your cousin would do: “I meant it as appreciation, but I realize I assumed traditional dress was encouraged. I should’ve checked first.”

**Yes, you’d be in the wrong if you exposed him in front of friends or family just to embarrass him. But you’re not wrong to call out the double standard.** Not voting doesn’t disqualify him from having political opinions. Blaming other people for not voting while repeatedly putting off registering himself is what makes this grating.

Since you’ve both laughed about it, he may not realize it’s stopped being funny to you. Tell him privately: “I’m not going to announce your voting history to your family. But when you blame people for not voting while you haven’t registered yourself, it bothers me. What’s actually keeping you from registering? And if you’re choosing not to vote, I’d like you to stop shaming other people for making the same choice.”

Then stop joking about exposing him. If he starts up in company, you can push back on the argument without revealing his history: “I don’t think it’s fair to pin the election on those voters.” You don’t have to sit there and nod, and you don’t have to manage his registration for him. What’s worth paying attention to is whether he takes you seriously when you tell him why this bothers you.

**Wearing a cheongsam wasn’t inherently disrespectful, but you made an assumption about what the hosts wanted.** A rehearsal dinner that incorporates Chinese traditions isn’t necessarily an invitation for guests to dress to a theme. The invitation said “cocktail formal.” A cheongsam can fit that dress code, but knowing the bride and her relatives would wear them wasn’t the same as knowing they wanted other guests to join in.

The detail I’d look at more closely is what you mean by doing your hair and makeup “in an Asian manner.” If you took inspiration from a specific hairstyle or makeup look, that’s different from trying to make yourself look East Asian. The latter can come across as caricature, even if you meant it as appreciation.

The bride’s mother complimented you, and there’s no reason to discount that. Likewise, a few stares don’t prove anyone was offended, and your cousin’s concern doesn’t tell you how the bride felt. Since the wedding is still ahead, I’d keep it low-key with your cousin: “I meant it as appreciation, but I realize I assumed the traditional dress was something guests were invited to join in on. I should’ve checked.” Then follow the wedding dress code without making the bride field a request for reassurance.

**Yes, you’d be in the wrong if you exposed him just to embarrass him. But you’re not wrong to call out the double standard.**

The edit matters. He doesn’t have to vote to understand policy or have a valid political opinion. But criticizing other people for not voting while repeatedly putting off registering himself is hypocritical. It makes sense that hearing him do that, while you’re the only one who knows, has gotten old.

Tell him privately, outside of a political debate, and drop the jokes about exposing him. You could say: “I’ve joked about this, but it actually bothers me. When you blame other people for not voting, you’re holding them to a standard you don’t meet. Is there something keeping you from registering that we haven’t talked about?”

Whether he registers is his decision. You don’t have to keep reminding him, cover for him, or sit through another rant. If he starts shaming nonvoters in front of friends, you can push back on what he’s saying without announcing his voting history: “I don’t think it’s fair to lecture people about why they didn’t vote.” That lets you challenge the behavior without turning his embarrassment into the point.

**You’re not wrong to call out the double standard, but I wouldn’t expose him in front of friends or family just to embarrass him.** The issue isn’t that he talks politics without voting. It’s that he blames other people for not voting while giving himself a pass.

Have one direct conversation without the running joke: “I’m going to stop nagging you to register. That’s your choice. But when you blame other people for not voting, knowing you don’t vote either, it bothers me. What’s keeping you from registering? And if you choose not to, I want you to stop shaming other people for making the same choice.”

If he does it again in company, you don’t have to sit there and nod. You can say, “I don’t think it’s fair to blame whole groups of people for not voting,” without revealing his voting history. And if someone asks you directly whether he votes, you don’t owe him a lie; you can say, “That’s a question for him.”

You’ve already tried reminders. At this point, what’s worth finding out is whether he can hear your concern and own the inconsistency—not whether embarrassment will finally get him to register.

**NTA for not having told her.** You didn’t create this situation, and you’re allowed to take time to decide what to do. But if you’re sure it’s an affair and you can tell her safely, I’d lean toward telling her privately. She deserves the chance to make her own decisions about her marriage.

It’s understandable to worry about the child. But finding out about an affair doesn’t automatically mean someone loses custody, and you don’t have to predict what she’ll do with the information. Telling her privately is also very different from exposing him to his employer, family, or the public.

Before reaching out, separate what the screenshots actually establish from what you’re inferring. If they’re clear, send one brief, factual message: “You don’t know me, but I saw some posts involving your spouse that I thought you’d want to know about. I can share what I saw if you’d like.” Don’t send intimate material, threaten anyone with the screenshots, or press her to respond. If there’s a credible risk of violence or retaliation, pause and get advice on how to handle it safely.

You can give her the information without taking responsibility for what happens to the marriage.

**YTA, mildly.** It wasn’t rude to want your pizza delivered to your door, and it wasn’t rude for him to ask if you could meet him downstairs. The rude part was turning a simple request into “do it my way or lose most of your tip.”

There’s a difference between offering a few extra bucks for climbing four flights and threatening to leave little or nothing because he asked for a favor. You may have meant it as banter, but he was working and had to take the offer seriously. And he didn’t put you in that situation: you could’ve just said, “Sorry, could you bring it up?”

Next time, either meet the driver downstairs or ask for door delivery and tip for the extra effort. No need to make it a negotiation at the bottom of the stairs.

**NTA for not having told her.** You didn’t create this situation, and you’re allowed to take time to decide whether getting involved would help. But if you have clear, credible evidence and can tell her safely and privately, I’d lean toward telling her. She deserves the chance to make her own decisions about her marriage.

A marriage ending isn’t the same as a parent losing their child. You don’t know what she’d choose or what would happen with custody, and you don’t have to make that choice for her. At the same time, screenshots prove what someone posted, not necessarily that every claim in the posts is true. Be clear about what you know firsthand and what you’re inferring.

If you reach out, keep it to one private, factual message: “I don’t know you, but I’ve seen posts from someone I know that appear to describe an ongoing relationship with your spouse. I can share what I saw if you want. I don’t know the full story, and you don’t owe me a response.” Don’t post the screenshots publicly, contact anyone’s employer, or send intimate images. If you have a concrete reason to fear violence or retaliation, pause before contacting anyone.

The best reason to tell her is to give her information she can use—not to punish either person or decide what should happen to their family.

**NTA for not telling her.** You didn’t create the situation, and you’re not responsible for managing the fallout. But if you have credible evidence, telling her privately would also be reasonable. She has a stake in knowing what’s happening in her own marriage.

I’d separate two things before deciding:

- **What do the screenshots actually establish?** If they clearly identify the married person and substantiate the affair, that’s different from suggestive posts or your acquaintance’s claims. If the evidence is ambiguous, don’t present it as proof.
- **What consequences are you assuming?** A breakup could be painful for the child, but disclosure doesn’t automatically mean the married parent loses custody or contact. And telling the wife privately is very different from exposing someone to their employer or posting about it publicly.

If the evidence is clear and you choose to tell her, I’d send one private, factual message: “You don’t know me, but I saw posts that appear to involve your spouse. I thought you should have the option to see them.” Share only what’s relevant, then let her decide what to do. Don’t involve the child, contact the workplace, or use the screenshots as leverage.

If you decide not to get involved, that’s defensible too. I’d stop collecting screenshots rather than keep yourself on standby. The decision is whether to give her information she can use—not whether to punish the people having the affair or protect them from every possible consequence.

**Mild YTA.** Wanting the pizza delivered to your door wasn’t the problem. The driver asked you for a favor, and you were free to say no. The rude part was telling him you’d cut his tip if he took you up on coming downstairs. What felt like banter to you probably landed as “climb four flights or lose most of your tip.”

He didn’t put you in a bad spot by asking, any more than you would’ve by saying, “Sorry, could you bring it up?” If $5 was meant as *extra* for the stairs, that’s a reasonable offer—just frame it as “I’ll tip extra for the climb,” not “I won’t tip if I come down.”

No need to make this a bigger deal than it is. Next time, mention the broken elevator in the delivery notes, ask plainly for door delivery, and tip with the extra effort in mind.

A mild YTA for not checking in, not for buying the computer. You can be right that the $500 won’t put you in a bad financial position and she can still reasonably want a heads-up before you turn a $200 repair into a $500 upgrade. With maternity leave and childcare costs still uncertain, the issue is less “Can we afford this PC?” and more “Have we agreed on what we can each spend without checking in?”

You’ve already apologized, which is a good first step. Rather than guessing how angry she is or trying to prove the purchase was affordable, ask what worried her most. Then make a budget together that includes a scenario where her leave is cut short, and agree on a spending threshold that applies to both of you. That way neither of you has to ask permission for every purchase, and neither gets surprised by a bigger one.

A little bit, yeah. Not for wanting the pizza brought to your door, but for making a low tip the consequence of him asking you a favor.

He didn’t put you in a bind just by asking. You could’ve said, “I’d rather you bring it up, thanks.” Four flights with a broken elevator is a fair reason for him to ask, and if door delivery is what you ordered, it’s fair for you to decline. It’s also reasonable to tip extra for the climb. The part that landed poorly was framing it as “come up or I’ll barely tip you,” rather than “I’ll tip extra if you bring it up.” You may have meant it as banter, but he was working and had to take the money part seriously.

You didn’t literally force him, and this isn’t a huge moral failing. Next time, just ask for door delivery and tip what you think the effort warrants, without dangling the tip.

A little, yes—for making the $500 decision without a heads-up, not necessarily for buying the computer. Nothing you’ve said establishes that you put your family in a bad financial position. But “we can afford it” and “we should talk before spending it” are two different questions.

From your perspective, it was a $300 upgrade over a repair you already needed. From hers, it may have been a discretionary purchase made while she’s trying to figure out what maternity leave and childcare will mean for your budget. You don’t have to guess which part bothered her most; you can ask.

You’ve already apologized, which is a good start. Next, sit down together and work out what you want to set aside before the baby comes, how the PC payoff fits into that plan, and what kinds of purchases you’ll both check in about. The goal isn’t to ask permission for every purchase. It’s to agree on which decisions are yours to make individually and which ones you want to make together.

**You were probably in the wrong for making the upgrade without a heads-up, not necessarily for buying the computer.** If the PC already needed a $200 repair, the choice was whether to spend an extra $300 for a better machine. That may be a reasonable deal. Nothing you’ve shared establishes that it put you in a bad financial position, though having savings and a previously empty credit card doesn’t settle what you can comfortably afford during maternity leave.

Her concerns about leave and childcare are reasonable even if the PC will be paid off before the baby arrives. And rather than assuming she’s angry, you can ask what bothered her most: the cost, the timing, or finding out after you’d already paid.

Apologizing for not consulting her was a good step. The useful follow-up is to look at the baby budget together, including what happens if her leave is shorter than planned, and agree on what each of you can spend independently and what warrants a check-in. The goal isn’t to ask permission for every purchase; it’s to agree on which decisions affect the plan you’re making together.

NTA for not *wanting* to visit. You can love your family without feeling the same urgency they do, and the cost of travel and missed work is real. Your mom isn’t wrong to ask, either: with the house being sold and your grandmother getting older, “I’ll visit when I get back” may not be quite the same option.

Since you’ll probably go anyway, I’d make it a visit you choose rather than one you feel guilted into. If you can only spare a few hours, think about what you’d most regret missing and prioritize that. Maybe that’s time with your grandmother, or maybe it’s seeing the house with your mom one last time. You don’t have to fit everyone in. If the fare is the main obstacle, it’s okay to ask if someone can help with it or meet you partway.

You could tell your mom: “I hear why this matters to you. I’m stretched thin with work and saving for Denmark, but I can make time for a short visit. I’d rather talk about what we can make work than whether I care enough.”

**NTA for not feeling like visiting.** You’re working hard to afford a year abroad, and a visit costs you both the fare and potentially a shift. It’s also understandable that your mom’s approach left you feeling guilty rather than excited to go.

That said, your mom has a point about what can’t necessarily wait. You can see most of your family when you get back, but the house may be sold by then, and you may not get another chance to see your grandmother. You don’t have to feel a strong urge to visit for it to be a choice you’re glad you made.

Since you’re leaning toward going anyway, I’d make it a visit you can afford rather than a tour of everyone you’re expected to see. Could you visit your grandmother on a day off and ask your mom and uncle to meet you there? If the fare is the sticking point, it’s reasonable to ask whether someone can pick you up or help cover it.

You could tell your mom, “I heard you about Grandma and the house. I’m trying to make a visit work around my shifts and budget. I’d rather talk about what’s doable than whether I care enough.”

**Yes, a little, if you take it down without asking.** You’re not wrong to be tired of seeing it on the shared mailbox, but seven months doesn’t tell you whether the cat was found or whether the owner still wants the flyer up.

I’d send a short text that gives them room to say the cat is still missing: “Hi, I moved in recently and noticed your lost-cat flyer on the shared mailbox. Is it still current? If you’re still looking, would you mind moving it to another spot?”

That might feel awkward, but it’s kinder than quietly removing it. If they don’t respond and the flyer is deteriorating or there are rules about posting on the mailbox, ask whoever manages the shared mailbox to handle that one. There’s no need to take down the others.

**NTA for not feeling like visiting.** You’re working hard to save for Denmark, and the fare and lost wages are real costs. Wanting to spend some of your remaining free time with friends doesn’t mean you don’t care about your family.

That said, “I can visit afterwards” doesn’t quite answer two of your mom’s points. The house may be sold by then, and another visit with your grandmother isn’t guaranteed. It makes sense that the conversation left you feeling guilty, but that feeling doesn’t mean you owe everyone a visit. It’s worth asking yourself which goodbye, if any, you’d wish you’d made time for.

Since you’re leaning toward going anyway, I’d see if you can make one short trip on a day off, prioritizing your grandmother and stopping by the house if that matters to you or is a gesture you want to make for your mom. You don’t need to fit in a farewell tour. If the trip would put a real dent in your savings, set up a proper call with your grandmother before you leave rather than counting on next year.

You can take your mom’s concerns seriously without letting guilt decide the whole itinerary.

You handled the meeting better than you handled the original conflict. You listened even when you were annoyed, apologized, and agreed to a leadership split that lets you keep doing what the team values about your tournament work. Keeping the tournament uniform while giving people more freedom at weekend games sounds like a sensible compromise.

The most important part of the update isn’t the sponsorship. Madison told you she’d found a group where she felt she belonged, and she wanted to stay. You’d already welcomed her back before you knew she’d secured a deal. Keep that distinction clear: she doesn’t have to bring the team free gear to earn her place.

You also don’t have to become a hugging person. But when a teammate gets emotional, try to hear what they’re telling you rather than writing it off as “hugging and crying.” The best follow-through now is to apply the new rules consistently and talk to people about problems before jumping to removal.

A mild YWBTA if you take down the flyer without asking. You’re not wrong to want an old flyer off the shared mailbox, but seven months tells you how long it’s been up, not whether the cat was found or whether the owner still wants it there. And the mailbox being in front of your house doesn’t make it yours alone.

You don’t have to ask whether the cat was found. Just ask about the flyer: “Hi, there’s a missing-cat flyer on the shared mailbox in front of our townhouse. Are you still using it, or would it be okay if I took it down?”

If they still want it up, you could ask whether there’s a better spot for it. If you don’t hear back and it’s deteriorating, ask whoever manages the shared mailbox about their posting rules. There’s no need to make a decision about every flyer in the neighborhood when only one is bothering you.

The best part of this update isn’t the sponsorship. It’s that you listened when you were annoyed, admitted you overreacted, and helped the team find a compromise: more freedom at casual games, consistent uniforms at tournaments, and shared leadership.

One thing to keep working on: take Madison seriously when she tells you what the team meant to her. You don’t have to be comfortable with tears or hugs to hear what she was saying. She’d found a group where she felt accepted, and she thought she was losing it. That’s a better read of the moment than “I guess we have to adjust to crying at meetings.”

If you haven’t already, a brief follow-up could help: “I’m glad you’re back. I should’ve talked with you before kicking you off. And I want you to know I’d feel that way even if the sponsorship hadn’t happened.”

Then put the new expectations in writing for everyone, including how you’ll handle disagreements before they turn into expulsions. That’s how you make this a lasting change rather than just a good meeting.

You were wrong to kick Madison off, but you handled the meeting better than you handled the dismissal. You let someone else lead even though it annoyed you, listened to Madison, and apologized in front of the team. The new arrangement sounds like a sensible compromise: keep the coordination you’re good at for tournaments, and give people more room to have fun at casual games.

The clearest sign you got the apology right is that you welcomed Madison back **before** you knew about the sponsorship. The free pellets are a nice bonus, not a reason she deserved to stay. And when she told you what it meant to find a group where she felt welcome, you didn’t need to decide whether her past experiences were really that bad. You just needed to hear what being on this team meant to her.

One useful follow-through would be to write down which requirements are for safety, which are for tournaments, and what happens when someone doesn’t meet them. For a non-safety issue, a private conversation should come before removal. That way the next person gets the benefit of what you learned here, too.

And you don’t have to become a hugger. Being willing to listen when someone gets emotional is enough.

I’d text the owner before taking down the flyer on the shared mailbox. Seven months is long enough to ask whether an old flyer still needs to be there, but it doesn’t tell you whether the cat was found. And the mailbox is shared, even if it’s right in front of your house.

You don’t have to ask what happened to the cat. Try: “Hi, I just moved in and noticed the lost-cat flyer on our shared mailbox. Are you still using it? It’s looking a little weathered, so I wanted to check before removing it.”

If they’re still looking, you could ask whether they’d move it to a community noticeboard or another spot where people will see it. If you don’t hear back and the flyer is deteriorating, check with whoever maintains the mailbox about removing it. Wanting that one flyer gone is reasonable; quietly taking it down without checking would be the inconsiderate part.

Going to rehearsal sounds like the right call. You’re not wrong for wanting a day at the water park, but skipping an important rehearsal before several gigs would affect the rest of the band. And while you’ll still get to see your friend on weekends, this is your last chance to play together before she leaves for college. That’s a different kind of goodbye.

Tell her what you said here: that she helped make the band what it is. That’ll probably mean a lot to her. And if your friends are up for it, pick another day for the water park.

I think you made the right call. Wanting to go to the water park doesn’t make you an asshole, but skipping an important rehearsal for it would be inconsiderate when the band is counting on you and has gigs coming up.

And even if you’ll see your friend on weekends, this is still your last rehearsal together before she leaves. That’s a moment you can’t reschedule the way you can a water-park trip. If it feels right, tell her what you told us: she helped make the band what it is, and you’ll miss playing with her.

I think you made the right call. Wanting to go to the water park doesn’t make you an asshole, but if the band was counting on you to rehearse for upcoming gigs, skipping would’ve left them to work around your absence.

And even if you’ll see your friend on weekends, this is still her last rehearsal with the band before college. That’s a different kind of goodbye. If it feels right, tell her something specific you appreciate about what she brought to the band. Then see if your friends are up for another water park day.

**You weren’t wrong to say up front that you wouldn’t change diapers. The mistake was agreeing to babysit without a plan for who would.** Your mom shares responsibility for that: she knew your limit and should have arranged backup rather than assuming you’d do it if she ran late. Even if she’d been back on time, though, a toddler could have needed a change within those three hours.

Once the boy’s pants were wet, the immediate issue was his comfort, not who’d won the argument. Calling your mom was a reasonable first step. When she couldn’t get back promptly, the next step was to find someone who could take over. Once your dad got home, he could have changed the child himself instead of yelling at you to do it. If you left knowing your dad had taken over, that’s different from leaving the kids without a responsible adult.

For next time, make the boundary about the whole job: **“I can help while you’re here, but I can’t be the sole caregiver for kids in diapers.”** Living rent-free can reasonably come with an expectation that you help out, but it doesn’t mean you have to accept every task.

The distress you describe sounds real. If worries about germs are making everyday activities exhausting or limiting what you can do, it may be worth talking with a mental health professional—not because you owe anyone diaper changes, but because you deserve to have those worries take up less of your day.

**ESH, but for different reasons.** You weren’t wrong to say up front that you wouldn’t change diapers. Your mom agreed to watch two toddlers and knew your limit a week in advance. She should have arranged backup instead of assuming she’d be home before either child needed a change. Living rent-free doesn’t erase the boundary you stated.

Where you went wrong was taking on sole care without a plan for a predictable need. Even if your mom had been home on time, a toddler could have needed a change within those three hours. Once the child’s pants were wet, calling your mom was a reasonable first step. When she couldn’t come back promptly, the priority was getting another adult to take over and change him. When your dad got home, you could have asked him directly to do it and made sure he was taking over before you left.

Your distress around germs sounds real. You don’t have to prove otherwise by agreeing to babysit again. Next time, make the boundary about the whole job: “I can help while you’re here, but I can’t be the only adult responsible for a child in diapers.” And if worries about contamination regularly interrupt cooking, socializing, or other things you want to do, it may be worth talking with a mental health professional about how much distress they cause you.

**You weren’t wrong to say up front that you wouldn’t change diapers. You were wrong to take the babysitting shift without a plan for who would, and your mom shares responsibility for leaving you in that position.**

You gave her a week’s notice about your limit. She’d agreed to watch the boys, so she shouldn’t have left without confirming that someone would handle diaper changes. But even if she’d been back on time, a two-year-old could need a change within three hours. Once you were the adult watching them, the job wasn’t just snacks and cartoons: if you couldn’t change a diaper, you needed to arrange for someone who could take over promptly.

Calling your mom was a reasonable first step. But once it was clear she wasn’t coming back soon, the priority was getting the child out of wet clothes, not settling who’d agreed to what. When your dad arrived, the most useful thing to say would have been, “I’m not able to do this. He’s been wet since around one. Not for wanting a say in who comes over. But making your girlfriend’s friends get your approval before they can visit a home you both live in is unfair, even if some of your concerns about specific guests are reasonable.

But being a little obnoxious isn’t the same as being unsafe, and inviting two people doesn’t have to mean inviting the whole group. Take her at her word that she hasn’t minded, without treating that as a reason to keep the arrangement by default. A fair starting point is that either of you can invite a friend over with a heads-up, neither invites extra people without checking, and you discuss specific safety or business concerns together. Apply the same rules to your friends. You can protect your home without making your girlfriend ask permission to use hers.

Your embarrassment is understandable, especially because you wanted to show up for a close friend, but it isn’t evidence that she’s judging you.

A short reply would be enough: “Thanks for understanding. I’m sorry I said I’d donate and didn’t let you know when I realized I couldn’t swing it this time. I hope the event went well.”

You don’t need to explain your expenses, stretch your budget, or promise another donation to make up for it. Next time, it’s fine to say, “I’d love to contribute if my budget allows,” and confirm once you know.

Yes, disappearing for a month without contacting your son was wrong. **Needing a break wasn’t the problem; cutting off contact was.** He was with his dad, so you didn’t leave him without care. But after a hospitalization and a period of intense distress, a month of silence from you may have felt like abandonment. His dad has reason to be upset, but that doesn’t make you a horrible person. It means there’s something important to repair.

Start with an apology that doesn’t ask your son to comfort you or forgive you: “I was overwhelmed, but it was my responsibility to get help and stay in touch. I’m sorry I disappeared. You don’t have to talk to me right now. I want to earn back your trust by showing up.” If he doesn’t respond, give him space without disappearing again. Keep the commitments you make, even small ones.

Talk to his dad separately and coordinate with your son’s treatment team. Tell them about the distress and property destruction, and ask for a plan for what to do if things escalate again. Breaking things needs a safety response, but it’s also worth revisiting the ban on seeing his friend. You didn’t know what happened between them, and the friendship clearly mattered to him. When he’s ready, listen to what it meant to him and what happened before deciding what boundaries are needed. If anyone is in immediate danger, seek emergency help.

You need support, too. Arrange respite with his dad or other trusted adults *before* you reach your limit again, with a clear plan for who’s caring for him and when he’ll hear from you. You can take a break and still be a parent he can count on.

Yes—leaving for a month with no contact was wrong. **Needing a break wasn’t wrong; cutting off contact was.** You sound exhausted, and having his dad care for him meant he wasn’t left without a parent. But your son was already struggling after a hospitalization, and your absence could have felt like you were withdrawing from him when things got hard. His dad also had to handle the situation without being able to reach you. That’s something to take responsibility for, not proof that you’re a horrible person.

Start with an apology that doesn’t ask your son to reassure you or forgive you: “I was overwhelmed, but I should have made a plan with your dad and stayed in touch. I’m sorry I disappeared. You don’t have to talk about it now. I’ll give you space, and I’ll keep showing up.” Then follow through. Apologize to his dad separately and agree on how you’ll share responsibilities and arrange breaks before either of you hits a wall.

Breaking things is a real safety concern, not just a tantrum. You and his dad should tell his mental-health team what happened and ask for a plan for future escalations. If anyone is in immediate danger, get to safety and seek emergency help. And unless there’s a specific safety concern about the friend, revisit the blanket ban: you know the conflict upset your son, but you don’t yet know what happened or whether cutting off contact helped. Give him a chance to explain when he’s ready, without making that conversation a condition of your apology.

Yes, leaving for a month without contacting your son was wrong. **Needing a break wasn’t the problem; disappearing was.** You made sure he was with his dad, which matters. But after a hospitalization and a distressing conflict, a month of silence could have felt like you’d given up on him. You can take responsibility for that without accepting that you’re a horrible person.

Start with an apology that doesn’t ask him to comfort you or forgive you: “I was overwhelmed, but it was my responsibility to get help and stay in touch. I left without explaining and didn’t contact you for a month. That wasn’t your fault. I’m sorry. You don’t have to talk to me right now. I’ll show you that you can count on me.” Then make small promises you can keep. If he doesn’t respond, give him room without going silent again.

Talk privately with his dad and reach out to your son’s treatment team. Tell them about the distress, the property destruction, and the month you were gone. Ask for help making a plan for future escalations. Breaking things needs a safety response, but it doesn’t tell you what the friendship meant to him or what happened between them. Rather than making him defend the friendship or explain the fight, let him know you’re willing to listen when he’s ready. If anyone is in immediate danger, seek emergency help.

You need support too. Plan breaks with his dad or another trusted adult *before* you hit your limit, with a clear handoff and a predictable way to stay in touch. The repair won’t come from finding the perfect explanation for why you left. It’ll come from showing up consistently now.

**YTA for how you handled it, not for wanting the used napkin off the kitchen table.** “Could you toss that? I don’t want used tissues on the table” is a reasonable request. Calling her nasty for coughing in her own room, then loudly calling her out in the kitchen, made it personal when it didn’t need to be.

Your usual roasting dynamic explains why you didn’t realize the jokes were landing differently. But when you asked if she was mad, she told you why. From what you described, she got tearful and answered your question; that isn’t the same as blowing up at you. You didn’t have to know beforehand that she was hurt. The part you could control was how you responded once she told you. “I’m sorry my joke affected you that much” made her reaction sound like the problem.

Wait until you’re sober and rested, then try a clean apology: “I’m sorry I called you nasty and got defensive when you told me it hurt. I could’ve just asked you to throw the napkin away. I’ll stop making jokes about you being sick.” Then give her room to respond without asking her to reassure you.

And yes, you pay for Hulu and can decide who uses it. But changing the password mid-watch because you were upset was a jab, not a boundary. Own that separately. Later, if you still want to talk about how you both bring up problems earlier, you can—but don’t make that a condition of apologizing.

**AITA verdict: Yes, for how you spoke to her and how you reacted when she told you it hurt—not for wanting the used napkin off the kitchen table.** That’s a reasonable hygiene request. “Hey, can you toss that?” would’ve handled it without calling her nasty or making a loud comment in front of her boyfriend.

Your usual roasting explains why you thought the first joke would land. You weren’t supposed to read her mind. But when you asked if she was mad, **she did tell you what was bothering her.** From what you described, she said she felt picked on and got tearful; that doesn’t sound like she blew up at you. It can sting to learn that a friend has been hurt for a while, but that doesn’t mean she was accusing you of being a bad person.

Your apology put the focus on how strongly she reacted instead of on what you said. And while Hulu is yours to share or not, changing the password mid-watch because you were upset was a retaliatory move. If you don’t want to share the account, make that a separate decision.

When you’re sober and rested, try a short apology without asking her to reassure you:

> “I’m sorry I called you nasty and got defensive when you told me it hurt. I could’ve asked you to toss the napkin without making a scene. I also changed the Hulu password because I was upset, and that was petty. I’ll stop making jokes about you being sick.”

Then give her some space. You can keep a reasonable standard for the shared kitchen without making her feel like being sick is something she has to apologize for.

**YTA for how you spoke to her and how you reacted when she told you it hurt.** You weren’t wrong to ask her to throw away a used napkin she’d left on the shared kitchen table. “Hey, can you toss that?” would’ve solved the problem without making her feel gross for being sick.

Your usual roasting explains why you thought “ya nasty” would land as a joke. It doesn’t mean she has to take it that way, especially after a month of feeling awful. And from your description, she didn’t blow up at you: you asked if she was mad, and she answered honestly, with tears in her eyes. That was her doing the thing you’d asked her to do—telling you when you’d hurt her. Your response made it sound like the problem was that she was too sensitive, not that you’d spoken harshly.

You’re allowed to decide who uses your Hulu. Changing the password midstream *because* you were upset was petty, though. Own that separately from whether you want to keep sharing it.

When you’re sober, give her a clean apology without asking her to reassure you or explain why she didn’t speak up sooner. Something like: “I’m sorry I called you nasty and snapped at you in the kitchen. When you told me I’d been upsetting you, I got defensive instead of listening. Changing the Hulu password while you were watching was petty, too. I’ll stop making jokes about you being sick, and if something bothers me in a shared space, I’ll just ask directly.”

You don’t have to decide you’re a bad person to admit you handled this badly. The repair is to hear her now and change how you bring things up next time.

You’re not an asshole for wanting to break up or for thinking about timing. But if you already know you’re done, I’d tell her soon, before prom, rather than wait until summer. Waiting a few days to find a private moment when neither of you has to rush back to class is considerate. Waiting weeks so you can go to prom as a couple takes away her chance to make her own plans knowing where things stand.

Being honest that you don’t know what the long-term future holds is different from telling her you’ve decided to end the relationship now. And you don’t need her to weigh the pros and cons or agree with you. She may be upset, and you can hear her out without turning the breakup into a debate.

You could say: “I care about you, and I’ve thought about this for a while. I’m not happy in the relationship anymore, and I’ve decided to end it. I know prom is coming up, and I’m sorry this changes our plans. I didn’t want to go together pretending I felt differently.”

You don’t need to list her medical issues or rehash your fights to justify leaving. Wanting more independence and knowing you don’t want to stay are enough. Seeing each other at school afterward may be awkward, but there’s a middle ground: choose a considerate moment soon, not a perfect moment months from now.

You’re not an asshole for wanting to break up or for taking a little time to figure out how to do it. But if you’ve already decided, I’d tell her soon rather than waiting until after prom or the start of summer. A few days to find a private moment is considerate; spending weeks acting like you’re still invested is more likely to leave her feeling blindsided.

Your edit matters: you haven’t promised her a future. But there’s a difference between “I don’t know where we’ll end up” and “I know I want to end this.” Telling her before prom lets her decide what she wants to do about the night, even if that means changing plans you were both looking forward to.

She doesn’t have to calmly discuss the pros and cons, and she doesn’t have to agree. She can be upset and you can still be kind and clear. I’d avoid making it about her medical issues or listing everything she’s done wrong. You could say:

> “I care about you, and these last few years have meant a lot to me. But I’ve realized I don’t want to continue the relationship. I know the timing is hard with prom coming up, but I didn’t want to go together without being honest with you.”

If you’re genuinely undecided, take a short, defined period to think. But from what you’ve written, you sound decided about the relationship and unsure about the timing. The middle ground is to choose a decent moment soon, not wait for a moment when it won’t hurt.

**Soft YTA.** You weren’t wrong to ask about the return policy or to think $25 was steep. But you bought the charger for a three-day need, used it for those three days, and returned it once it had done its job. That’s closer to treating the store as a free rental service than returning something that didn’t work out.

The store honored its policy, so this isn’t a huge moral failing. And if the cashier had explicitly said, “Sure, use it for the trip and bring it back,” I’d see it differently. But explaining the return policy isn’t quite the same as agreeing to that arrangement.

**Soft YTA—unless you were upfront that you’d used it for three days and the store was fine with that.**

A $25 charger is frustrating when you only need it for a trip. But it did what you bought it to do, and it sounds like you asked about returns so you could use it for the vacation and then get your money back. That’s treating the return policy as a free rental, not returning something that didn’t work out.

That said, if you told the cashier it was used and they knowingly accepted it under the policy, I wouldn’t feel guilty. The key distinction is whether the store agreed to take back a used charger, not whether $25 was a fair price.

**Mild YTA if you bought it planning to use it for the trip and return it.** $25 for a charger you only need for a few days is frustrating, but a refund policy isn’t necessarily an offer to lend you one for free.

The cashier did say you could get a full refund with the receipt and packaging, so it’s reasonable that you took him at his word. If you told him you planned to use it for three days and he said that was fine, I’d say NTA. If you only asked about the general policy, though, the store accepting the return doesn’t quite settle whether it was fair to treat the purchase as a free rental.

Not a huge moral failing. Next time, I’d ask the hotel front desk if they have a loaner before paying the convenience markup.

You’re not an asshole for wanting to help Max, but I’d take back the offer to be his fake girlfriend. Trying to provoke a breakup puts you in the middle and could make things less safe if he’s genuinely afraid of her.

His girlfriend could be controlling, and he could also be handling things badly. Those aren’t mutually exclusive. You don’t have to decide whether his account is true to recognize that his history of cheating and his plan to make *her* end things are good reasons not to get involved.

You could say: “I care about you, but I’ve thought about it and I’m not going to pretend to date you. If you want to leave and you’re scared of how she’ll react, I’ll help you find someone who can help you make a safe plan.” A trusted friend, campus counselor, or relationship-abuse advocate could help him think through his options.

And if part of you hopes this might turn into something real, that doesn’t make you a bad person. It’s one more reason to step back while he’s still in a relationship.

You’re not wrong for wanting to break up, and taking a few days to choose a considerate time doesn’t make you an asshole. But if you’ve already decided, I’d lean toward telling her **before prom** rather than waiting until summer.

Waiting until school ends has a real upside: you wouldn’t have to see each other every day right after the breakup. But going to prom as a couple when you already know you want out could leave her feeling blindsided and take away her chance to make different plans. Your edit matters—you haven’t promised her a long-term future—but being uncertain about the future together is different from privately having decided to end things.

The middle ground is to pick a calm, private time in the next few days, rather than doing it tomorrow out of guilt or putting it off for weeks. Her medical issues can make the timing feel especially hard, but caring about her doesn’t obligate you to stay. And you don’t have to predict whether she’ll react calmly: if your decision is made, the conversation isn’t a debate she has to agree to. You can listen and be kind without making it sound negotiable.

You might say: “I care about you, and I’ve thought about this for a while. I’m not happy in the relationship anymore, and I’ve decided to end it. I know prom is coming up, and I wanted to tell you now so you have a say in what you do that night.”

You don’t need to list her faults or make her medical needs the reason. Be clear about the decision, give her room to react, and handle prom logistics separately if she needs time.

**You’re not an asshole for wanting to help him. But pretending to be his girlfriend to provoke a breakup would be a bad call.**

You don’t have to decide whether Max’s account of his girlfriend is true to know that this plan isn’t good for anyone. If she’s controlling and he’s afraid of how she’ll react, provoking her could make things less safe for both of you. And his admission that he’s repeatedly cheated while hoping she’ll end things is worth taking seriously: he’s asking you to join a pattern that hasn’t solved the problem.

You can take back the offer: “I care about you, but I’ve thought about it and I’m not going to pretend we’re dating. If you’re scared to leave, I’ll help you talk to someone you trust or find support through campus counseling.”

If part of you hopes this might turn into a real relationship, be honest with yourself about that, too. You don’t need to feel guilty for having feelings, but keep things platonic while he’s in a relationship. If he does end it, take your time deciding whether his choices make him someone you’d want to date.

You’re not an asshole for caring about Max or having feelings for him. But pretending to be his girlfriend so his actual girlfriend will find out and dump him would be a bad choice. You can take back the offer.

Max may be telling the truth about feeling controlled or afraid. You don’t have enough information to know, and you don’t need to settle that question to say no. If she is abusive, provoking a confrontation could make things less safe for him and pull you into it. If she isn’t, you’d be helping him deliberately hurt her so he doesn’t have to end the relationship himself. Either way, his admission that he’s cheated repeatedly and hopes she’ll find out is worth taking seriously, especially if you’re hoping to date him.

You could say: “I care about you, but I’ve thought it over and I’m not going to pretend to date you or help make her break up with you. If you’re scared to leave, I’ll help you find support.”

If he genuinely fears her reaction, a trusted friend, campus advocate, or relationship-abuse service can help him think through how to leave safely. And if part of you wants a real relationship with him, keep that separate: wait until he’s actually single, then ask yourself whether how he handled this relationship gives you reason to trust him in one with you.

Yes, you were in the wrong—not for asking once if she’d return the crib, but for treating her refusal as a debt and then withholding birthday and Christmas gifts to make a point.

$1,400 is a lot of money, and it’s understandable to wish you’d waited. But unless you agreed upfront that the items were loans or conditional gifts, they became hers when you gave them to her. Making a registry doesn’t amount to a promise that the pregnancy will continue, and she doesn’t owe you an explanation that makes you feel better about what you spent.

You’re not obligated to buy her more gifts. The distinction is between quietly setting a budget you’re comfortable with and retroactively declaring that the crib counts against her because she wouldn’t give it back.

If you want to repair things, drop the reimbursement request and say something like: “We were uncomfortable with how much we’d spent, and we took that out on you. The crib and clothes were gifts, and you don’t owe us anything. I’m sorry we pushed and brought birthdays and Christmas into it.” Next time, spend only what you’d be comfortable giving with no strings attached.

**YTA for demanding reimbursement, not for asking once whether she’d return the gifts.** $1,400 is a lot of money, so it’s understandable that you’d want to recover it if the items aren’t being used. But you gave her a crib and clothes, not a loan. Unless you agreed beforehand that she’d return them if her plans changed, she doesn’t owe you the items or the money.

Making a registry while expecting a baby doesn’t amount to a promise that the pregnancy will continue. Nothing you’ve described suggests she asked for gifts in bad faith. Once she said she wanted to keep them for the future, retroactively calling them her birthday and Christmas presents came across as a penalty, not a compromise. You’re free to spend less on future gifts without rewriting what you already gave her.

If you want to repair things, keep it short: “We were frustrated about how much we spent, but those were gifts. We shouldn’t have demanded repayment or tried to make them count for other occasions. I’m sorry.” Then let the matter rest rather than asking the family to take sides.

Yes, I think you were in the wrong—not for asking once if she’d return the items, but for demanding reimbursement after she said no.

$1,400 is a lot of money, and it’s understandable to wish you could get it back now that the crib and clothes won’t be used as soon as you expected. But unless you agreed beforehand that the gifts were conditional, they became hers when you gave them to her. Keeping them isn’t “holding your money hostage.” And making a registry after trying for years doesn’t show she misled you. Planning for a baby and later changing course when circumstances change are compatible.

You’re free to spend less on future birthday or Christmas gifts. That’s different from retroactively calling these her birthday and Christmas presents after she refused to pay you back. In that context, it’s likely to land as punishment, even if you meant it as a compromise.

I’d drop the reimbursement request and apologize directly: “We gave you those things as gifts, and we were wrong to pressure you to return them or pay us back. We’re sorry we made this harder.” If the family is still arguing over it, you can tell them you’ve dropped the issue and ask them not to take sides on your behalf.

**AITA verdict: Yes, for the comment—not for being worried about your teen.** It makes sense that you wish someone had warned you, and you don’t have to minimize what you went through. But a sarcastic remark about your ex’s diagnosis during a tense handoff, after their partner rolled their eyes, wasn’t the same as a thoughtful, private warning about specific behavior. It also didn’t address the problem your teen keeps bringing to you: getting attached to people and then having to deal with their absence.

You don’t know why this person stopped coming around. Feeling a little smug doesn’t make you a bad person, but I wouldn’t treat their absence as a win. If your teen misses them, you can say, “It makes sense that you miss them. You can talk to me about it, and you don’t have to take sides.” If your teen heard the comment, you can own it briefly: “That was a dig I shouldn’t have made at pickup. It’s not your job to sort it out.”

With your ex, bring up the pattern privately and make a concrete request: “When someone spends a lot of time with our teen and then stops coming around, our teen has a hard time. Can we agree to wait until a relationship is more established before a new partner becomes a regular part of their life?” That’s a more useful conversation than debating the diagnosis or whether the new partner needed a warning.

NTA for asking. You’re allowed to say when you don’t feel like being kissed, even if you usually enjoy it. But if these are quick, everyday kisses, your daughter’s giggling doesn’t necessarily mean she’s uncomfortable or that either of you is doing anything wrong. At 13, seeing your parents be romantic can just be funny.

Your wife may have heard “I’m embarrassed by you” when you meant “I feel self-conscious when we get laughed at.” You could tell her: “I love that you’re affectionate with me. I got embarrassed when she laughed, and I think I made it sound like you did something wrong. You didn’t.”

If you’d rather save longer kisses for private, that’s a reasonable preference to talk through. But if it’s a quick peck and the giggling is the only issue, you might try letting the moment pass rather than making a blanket rule around your daughter.

**Yes, for the comment—not for being worried about your teen.** It’s frustrating to be the one helping your kid through repeated goodbyes, and it makes sense that you wish someone had given you a heads-up before your own relationship. But a sarcastic remark after an eye roll, in the middle of a tense handoff, was more of a jab than a warning. Even with a confirmed diagnosis, the behaviors you experienced are what would make a warning useful—not the label alone.

You also don’t know why this person stopped coming around. The more useful question is what you can do about the pattern your teen is struggling with. You can own the remark without backing off that concern: “I shouldn’t have made that comment at pickup. Separately, our kid has been having a hard time when people they’ve gotten close to stop coming around. Can we talk about waiting until a relationship is more established before involving them?”

With your teen, keep it about their experience rather than why the person left: “It’s okay to miss them. You don’t have to pick sides or figure out what happened between the adults.” That gives your kid support without making them the go-between.

**NTA for asking.** You’re allowed to feel self-conscious and ask your wife to save kisses for when you’re alone. She may also have heard “I’m embarrassed by *you*,” even though what embarrasses you is being laughed at.

Your daughter’s laughter doesn’t necessarily mean she’s uncomfortable or that a quick kiss is inappropriate. At 13, she might just find it funny to see her parents being affectionate. You don’t have to change what you do just because she giggles—but you don’t have to pretend it doesn’t bother you, either.

Try telling your wife: “I love that you’re affectionate with me. When our daughter laughs, I get self-conscious. I’m not embarrassed by you, and I’m sorry it came across that way.” Then be specific about what you’d actually feel comfortable with: maybe a quick peck is fine but lingering kisses feel too public, or maybe you’d rather save kisses for private altogether. The point is to talk about your comfort without making either your wife’s affection or your daughter’s reaction the villain.

**Yes, you were out of line in that moment.** Your concern about your teen getting attached to people who then disappear is legitimate. But a sarcastic remark during a tense handoff wasn’t the same as a thoughtful warning. Even taking the NPD diagnosis as given, bringing it up that way put private information into a conflict and risked making handoffs more tense for your kid.

It makes sense that you wish someone had told you more before you got into that relationship, especially given what you’ve had to work through since. That doesn’t mean the jab came from pure spite, and it doesn’t mean it caused this person to stop coming around. You don’t know why they left.

I’d separate the apology from the parenting conversation. If you can communicate civilly, a simple “I shouldn’t have made that comment at drop-off. I’ll keep handoffs about our kid” owns your part without taking back your concerns. Later, raise the concrete pattern: “When someone spends a lot of time with our teen and then stops coming around, they’ve come to me upset and with questions. Can we agree to wait until a relationship is more established before including a new partner in regular family time?”

With your teen, let them miss the person without asking them to explain what happened or take sides. You can take their hurt seriously without making your ex’s diagnosis the explanation for it.

**Yes, you’d be in the wrong if you got the $300 reimbursement and kept it.** Your friend paid for the repair, and you passed his money to the person who did the work. Even if the reimbursement comes to you, it’s covering an expense he paid.

You don’t owe him $300 out of pocket while the reimbursement is still hypothetical. I’d tell him: “My landlady offered to reimburse the $300 if we can get an invoice. Can you ask the guy who did the work for one? If she reimburses it, I’ll pass the money back to you.”

It’s fair to be annoyed that he arranged work on your rental before your landlady approved it. And he still owes you $100 for the stay. But those are separate issues. If you’d both prefer to settle up by sending him $200 and calling the lodging balance paid, agree on that first rather than deducting it without telling him.

**Yes, you’d be the asshole if you got the $300 reimbursement and kept it without your friend’s agreement.** He gave you that money for a specific repair, and you passed it on to the person who did the work. If your landlady reimburses that expense, the money should go back to the person who actually covered it. If you never get the reimbursement, you don’t owe him $300 out of your own pocket.

It’s fair to be annoyed that he hit the roof and arranged for someone to work on it before your landlady approved it. But that’s a separate issue, as is the $100 he still owes you for his stay. You could say: “If I get the $300 back from my landlady, I’ll send it to you. You still owe me $100 for the stay—would you rather I send you $200 and call us square?” If he doesn’t agree to that, return the $300 and ask for the $100 separately.

**No, you’re not an asshole for asking.** You can enjoy kissing your wife and still feel self-conscious when your daughter laughs. Your wife isn’t wrong for enjoying ordinary affection in front of your daughter, either. Your daughter’s laughter doesn’t necessarily mean she’s uncomfortable or judging you; she might just find it funny to see her parents being mushy.

The distinction is between “I’d rather not kiss right now,” which is always okay, and “It’s inappropriate to kiss around our daughter,” which isn’t supported by what you’ve described. If your wife heard the request as “I’m embarrassed by you,” it’s worth clearing that up.

You could say, “I love that you’re affectionate with me. I get flustered when she laughs, but I’m not embarrassed to be with you. How did it land when I asked you to stop?” Then talk about what actually bothers you. If a quick peck feels fine but longer kisses make you self-conscious, say that. If you’d rather skip kissing in those moments altogether, you can say that kindly without making your wife’s affection the problem.

Yes—if your landlady reimburses the full $300 for that repair, you should pass it back to your friend. He was responsible for hitting the roof, and he covered the repair. You passed his money to the repairer, so you haven’t pocketed anything. But if the landlady reimburses that same expense, keeping the money would leave you $300 ahead on a bill your friend paid.

It’s fair to be annoyed that he arranged for someone to work on the roof before your landlady approved it. That put you in an awkward spot as the tenant. But that’s a separate issue, as is the $100 he still owes you for staying over. If you’d both prefer to settle everything in one transfer, ask whether he’s okay with you sending him $200 and counting the other $100 toward that balance.

For now, get an accurate invoice and wait until the reimbursement actually comes through. You don’t owe him $300 out of your own pocket while it’s still pending.

You’re not an asshole for being disappointed. A coffee maker six months after you quit coffee—when you already have two—is a reasonable thing to return. The part to own is the pouting: it tells your wife something’s wrong but leaves her guessing what.

Talk to her privately, away from the kids. You can keep it simple: “I’m sorry I’ve been sulking. Can we return the coffee maker? Since I don’t drink coffee anymore, I won’t use it. I think what I really wanted today was dinner together. Next year, can we do that instead of gifts?”

If the bigger hurt is that you wanted to feel known, it’s okay to say that too: “I know you were trying to do something nice. The gifts didn’t feel much like me, and that stung a little.” The $300 watch may explain why the difference in effort is on your mind, but leading with the price will make it harder to talk about what actually hurt.

And if you’ve been feeling low for reasons beyond today, tell her that separately. You don’t have to pretend the gift landed well, and you don’t have to make it carry everything else you’re feeling.

**NTA for being upset.** Your husband knew you were hard to wake and agreed to wake you. Asking once without checking that you were actually awake didn’t follow through on that promise. If he needed to leave so your son wouldn’t miss the trip, that’s understandable—but it doesn’t make “not my problem” a fair response afterward.

How you “kicked off” is a separate question. If you said something hurtful, you can apologize for that without apologizing for being disappointed. You could say: “I’m sad I missed his first trip. I relied on you because you said you’d wake me. Next time, can we agree that waking me means checking I’m sitting up and responding? If you can’t do that, please tell me the night before so I can make another plan.”

And if you haven’t already, ask your son to tell you his favorite part. It won’t replace being there, but you still get to share a little of the day with him.

**You’re not an asshole for being disappointed or wanting to return the coffee maker.** You quit drinking coffee, and there are already two other machines in the house. What seems to sting is that you expected your wife to know what would make you feel appreciated, and the gifts missed the mark. That’s worth talking about. Pouting, though, leaves her guessing.

You can ask for the return without turning it into a verdict on how much she cares:

> “I’ve been quiet because I felt disappointed and didn’t know how to say it without sounding ungrateful. Since I don’t drink coffee anymore, can we return the coffee maker? Honestly, I would’ve loved just having dinner together. Can we do that next year instead of gifts?”

Have that conversation privately with your wife. You’ve clarified that you don’t blame the kids, so there’s no need to make them part of it. I’d also leave the $300 watch out of the return conversation. If what’s bothering you is a broader mismatch in how much thought or effort you each put into these occasions, that’s a fair topic—but it isn’t about matching price tags.

You can be having a rough time *and* have a legitimate disappointment. You don’t have to sort out which feeling is bigger before asking for the receipt.

On what you’ve described, **your husband was in the wrong for not following through, and you’re not an asshole for being upset.** He agreed to wake you, knew it usually takes more than one attempt, and left without checking that you were actually awake. “Wake yourself up next time” might be a conversation worth having, but it doesn’t address the promise he made this time.

The part I can’t judge is “kicking off.” Telling him you’re hurt is fair; if you yelled or insulted him, you can apologize for that without taking back the point.

When things are calmer, you could say: “I’m sad I missed his first trip. I relied on you because you said you’d wake me. Next time, if you agree to help, can you make sure I’m actually awake before you leave? If you can’t do that, please tell me the night before so I can make another plan.” A backup alarm might help for future mornings, but needing a backup doesn’t make your disappointment unreasonable.

**You’re not an asshole for being disappointed.** A coffee maker is an odd fit when you quit coffee six months ago and already have two in the house. And if choosing sunglasses is something you enjoy doing yourself, it makes sense that a pair someone else picked wouldn’t land. It sounds like what stung was feeling like your preferences weren’t considered. That’s worth talking about, without assuming you know why your wife chose those gifts.

The pouting is the part to own. It signals that something’s wrong but leaves your wife guessing what. You can ask to return the coffee maker without turning it into a verdict on how much she cares:

> “I’m sorry I’ve been sulking instead of saying something. Can we return the coffee maker? Since I quit coffee and we already have two, I won’t use it. I was disappointed, and I realized what I really wanted for Father’s Day was dinner together. Next year, can we just plan that instead of doing gifts?”

The $300 watch may explain why the contrast felt sharp, but it doesn’t set a price your wife owed you. If there’s a broader mismatch in how you each like to celebrate or how much effort you expect, talk about that separately. And feeling low about other things doesn’t make this disappointment fake; it’s a good reason to take a moment before talking, not to keep a third coffee maker.

**NTA for being upset.** You missed a first you were looking forward to, and you’d made a plan with your husband: he said he’d wake you. Given that he knew how hard it is for you to wake up, one attempt and then “it’s not my problem” was dismissive. If he had to leave to get your son there on time, leaving may have been reasonable; that doesn’t erase the agreement or make your disappointment unreasonable.

“Kicking off” is a separate question. Telling him you were hurt and angry is fair. If it involved insults or yelling, you can apologize for how you spoke without taking back what upset you.

When things are calmer, you could say: “I relied on you because you said you’d wake me. Next time, if you can’t do that, please tell me the night before. If you can, let’s agree that waking me means making sure I’m actually awake.” A backup alarm you know works for you could help too—not because this was all on you, but because you don’t want to miss another moment that matters to you.

A little, yes—but it sounds like a thoughtless comment, not a deliberate dig. She brought up sex, so it makes sense that you heard it as an opening for some banter. The part that likely hurt was hearing “you’re lucky” alongside “I’m ovulating,” when you knew she hadn’t ovulated in months and had been trying to conceive for two years.

I’d text her back now rather than wait until you’ve settled the question of who was right. You can acknowledge that it hurt without pretending you meant to hurt her:

> I’m sorry. I was joking about our sex lives, but I didn’t think about how bringing up ovulation would land when I know what you’ve been going through. I can see why that hurt. I care about you, and I’ll be more thoughtful.

Then give her room to respond. You don’t have to avoid talking about your life altogether; this is about being more mindful of a specific sore spot.

A little, yes. It sounds like you meant to commiserate about mismatched sex drives, not rub anything in. But knowing she hasn’t ovulated in months and has been trying to conceive for two years, bringing up your own ovulation was a thoughtless comparison. Her mentioning sex didn’t necessarily mean she was up for talking about fertility.

You don’t need to decide whether you’re a bad friend to text her back. Just apologize for the specific comment:

> “I’m sorry I brought up ovulating. I was trying to relate to what you said about sex, but I knew what you’ve been going through and didn’t think about how that would land. I’m sorry I hurt you.”

Then give her room to respond. You don’t have to treat your own body or postpartum experience as taboo; this is about being more thoughtful about the timing and audience.

You weren’t wrong to talk about your sex life, but bringing up ovulation was a thoughtless moment. Your friend opened the door to talking about sex, so it makes sense that you responded with something from your own life. But sex and fertility aren’t quite the same topic. You knew she hadn’t ovulated in months and had been trying to conceive for two years, so hearing “I’m ovulating” from a friend who just had a baby could sting, even though you meant it as a comment about your libido.

I’d text her back and apologize for that specific remark. You don’t have to say you meant to hurt her to acknowledge that you did.

> “I’m sorry I brought up ovulating. I was trying to relate to what you said about sex, but I wasn’t thinking about how that would land, especially knowing what you’ve been going through. I care about you, and I’m sorry I hurt you.”

Then give her room to respond. A moment of insensitivity is something you can repair; it doesn’t make you a bad friend.

**A mild YTA for how you brought it up, not for wanting your parents to see the baby more.** You didn’t literally call your girlfriend a gold-digger, but saying “we shouldn’t take their money if they can’t see the baby” in an unrelated argument can sound like “you’re happy to take their money but won’t let them see her.” It also makes visits sound like something your parents are owed in return for helping.

Your disappointment is understandable. Her parents see the baby often because you live with them, but that’s different from packing up a seven-week-old and going somewhere. Instead of assuming she’s making excuses, ask what’s making visits hard right now. A short, planned visit where you handle the logistics might be easier, if she’s comfortable with it.

You could say: “I’m sorry I brought up the money in our argument. I don’t think you’re using my parents, and their help doesn’t buy them time with the baby. I do miss seeing them with her. Can we talk about what would make a visit manageable for both of us?”

It’s reasonable to reconsider accepting money if it comes with expectations you’re not comfortable with. Just make that a separate conversation from when and how your parents visit.

**NTA for asking, but your dad’s decision sounds fair.** If you understood the rule as “everyone has to be in the car by 7:10,” it makes sense that you thought it should apply to both of you. But your dad seems to be applying a different rule: *Who was ready to leave at 7:10?* If your brother was ready and waiting, closing your doors at nearly the same time doesn’t mean you both held up the departure.

Your mom can be right that the rule was ambiguous and still think you should own your part. You can acknowledge that you weren’t ready at 7:10 without conceding that the rule was clear. The initial question was reasonable; once your dad explained the distinction, arguing over the door timing probably wasn’t worth it.

When things cool down, you could say: “I thought the rule was about when we got in the car. I get now that you meant being ready to leave. Can we agree on where I’m supposed to be at 7:10 so there’s no confusion next time?”

You weren’t wrong to ask for clarification, but I think your dad’s call was reasonable based on what you described.

There’s a difference between **getting into the car at the same time** and **being ready to leave at the same time**. If your brother was ready at 7:10 and only got in at 7:11 because he was waiting, then closing the doors five seconds apart doesn’t mean you both held up the departure. And if your dad wasn’t ready at 7:10 either, it’s fair to ask how that affects the rule. Your mom’s right that it’s ambiguous.
