A gentle YTA for how you handled the conversation, not for being excited about your progress. “I wish I could lose weight” isn’t necessarily a request for advice. Once she said fasting didn’t sound healthy to her, that was a good point to let it go. In that context, “it’s also not healthy to be fat” could sound like a judgment of *her*, even if you meant it about yourself.

You already clarified what you meant. If things still feel awkward, a brief, private apology would do more than explaining your intent again: “Hey, I’m sorry I gave you unsolicited advice and made that comment about weight. I shouldn’t have put you in that position.” Then give her space and keep things friendly and professional.

You can be proud of what you’ve accomplished without turning what worked for you into advice for someone else.

**A little, yes—but you’ve already identified where you went wrong.** You were excited about your progress, and it makes sense that you wanted to share what worked for you. But “I wish I could lose weight” isn’t necessarily a request for advice. When she said she thought fasting was unhealthy, that was a good moment to let the subject drop.

Even though “it’s also not healthy to be fat” was about yourself, it came right after you suggested *she* fast. In that context, it could easily sound like a judgment about her body or a dismissal of her concern. Your clarification explained what you meant, but it didn’t undo how the exchange landed.

The next time you have a private moment, keep it brief: **“Hey, I’m sorry I gave you unsolicited advice about weight loss and made that comment. I should’ve dropped the subject.”** Then give her space and go back to being a friendly coworker. You can be proud of your progress without making it a plan for anyone else.

A mild YTA for how you handled the conversation, not for being proud of losing 60 pounds. You were excited to share what worked for you, and it’s good that you clarified right away that you were talking about yourself.

The trouble is that “I wish I could lose weight” isn’t necessarily a request for advice. And once she said fasting sounded unhealthy to her, “it’s also not healthy to be fat” could reasonably land as a judgment about *her*, even if you meant it as an explanation of your own choices. Higher weight can be associated with health risks, but that doesn’t tell you how healthy an individual coworker is or whether fasting is right for her.

If you get a private moment, a short apology is enough: “Hey, I’m sorry I gave you weight-loss advice you didn’t ask for and made that comment. I got carried away talking about what worked for me.” Then let it rest. You don’t need to explain your intent again or ask her to reassure you. Going forward, you can share your progress without turning it into a recommendation.

Explaining why an icon looks pixelated isn’t mansplaining by itself. Your employer raised a real concern, and you had relevant expertise. From what you’ve shared, there isn’t enough to say you were TA. The part worth examining is what “dumbing it down” looked like in practice: using less jargon is helpful; talking as if she couldn’t grasp something obvious can come across as condescending, even if you didn’t mean it that way.

Also, you could both have been right. A 200 × 200 px icon can look fine at its intended size and blurry when enlarged, and your employer was still right to flag what she saw. Instead of trying to get her to understand the technical explanation, you could make it easy to check the result: “This preview is larger than the icon will appear on the site. Can we check it at the intended size? If it still looks blurry there, I can provide a higher-resolution or vector version.”

I wouldn’t send an apology just because you’re replaying it late at night. If you remember a specific remark that sounded dismissive, a brief “I think I came across as dismissive earlier—sorry about that” is enough. And with your peers, it’s okay to set a limit on how much help you give rather than letting the frustration seep into how you explain things.

**Probably NTA for explaining, but “I had to dumb it down” is the part I’d rethink.** Explaining a technical issue someone asked about isn’t inherently mansplaining. The question is whether you treated her concern as valid or talked to her as if she couldn’t understand. From your description, there’s not enough to know how it landed, and her forwarding the work doesn’t tell you either way.

You and your employer may have been answering different questions. You were explaining *why* a 200×200 icon looks pixelated when enlarged; she was flagging that it *looked* pixelated. Both can be true. A more collaborative response would be: “I see the pixelation you’re pointing out. Do we know how large this icon will display on the site? If it needs to look sharp at a larger size or on a high-density screen, I can provide a higher-resolution version or an SVG.”

With peers, you don’t have to be the go-between just because they ask. “I can help you spot where you got stuck, but you’ll need to ask the teacher about that part” is a fair boundary.

Unless you remember saying something dismissive, I wouldn’t send a late-night apology over this. Take the useful lesson: **simplify the explanation without assuming anything about the person.**

**A little, yeah—for the joke, not for reconnecting with your mate.** You meant it as banter, but you’d just been talking about dates with *her*. In that context, “they don’t really live up to the hype” can sound like “being with her is disappointing,” even if you meant nothing of the sort.

Give her the night, and tomorrow try apologizing for how the joke landed rather than explaining the banter again: “I meant it as a throwaway joke, but I can see how it sounded like I was putting you down to my mate. I’m sorry. I love being with you, and I don’t want to make you the punchline.”

Her picking up your phone and reading your messages is a separate issue. If you haven’t agreed that’s okay, it’s fair to talk about privacy once things are calmer. One issue doesn’t cancel out the other.

And you don’t have to make her your *only* focus to show you appreciate that she moved for you. Reconnecting with old friends is healthy; you can do that without making your relationship the butt of the joke.

A little, yeah. You meant it as banter, but in a conversation about dates with your girlfriend, “they don’t really live up to the hype” can sound like you’re telling your mate that being with her is disappointing. The context explains why you said it; it doesn’t erase how it landed.

Let things cool off tonight. Tomorrow, try apologizing without asking her to agree it was funny: “I was joking with my mate, but I get why it sounded like I was putting you down. I’m sorry I said it. I love being with you, and I don’t think you or our relationship are a letdown.”

There’s a separate issue: if she picked up your phone and read your messages without permission, it’s fair to talk about privacy once you’ve addressed the hurt. You can own the joke without treating the phone-checking as okay.

And reconnecting with your mate isn’t the problem. You can appreciate how far she moved to be with you without making her your *only* focus. Having friendships outside your relationship is healthy.

Based on what you’ve described, I wouldn’t call it mansplaining. Your employer raised a concern about how the icons looked, and explaining why a small raster image gets blurry when enlarged was relevant. The part I can’t judge is your tone: simplifying an explanation is helpful; talking as if the other person is incapable of understanding is condescending. Your phrase “dumb it down” is worth reflecting on, but it doesn’t tell me how you actually spoke to her.

I also wouldn’t assume she didn’t get it. She may have understood the explanation and still been concerned about the result. A 200 × 200 icon can be fine at its intended size and still look blurry if it’s enlarged or doesn’t have enough pixels for how it’s displayed on a high-density screen. A useful way to handle it next time is: “What size will this icon appear at in the final layout? Let’s check it at that size. If it still looks soft, I can send an SVG or a higher-resolution export.” That takes her observation seriously and gives you both a way to resolve it.

As for your peers, if they ask for help, explaining is fine. If you’re tired of being the go-to person, it’s also fine to say, “I can help with this part, but ask the teacher about the rest.” You don’t have to keep helping until you’re frustrated.

Unless you remember a specific remark that came out patronizing, I wouldn’t read her silence as a reason to apologize. If you do remember one, a quick “I think I sounded dismissive earlier—sorry about that” is enough.

**No, you wouldn’t be an asshole for adopting a cat after rehoming your husky.** You recognized that your new schedule wasn’t working for him, took care choosing a home, and are glad he’s thriving even though you miss him. Adopting another animal wouldn’t undo that or mean you loved him any less.

The question is whether **this particular cat** would do well with your schedule. A healthy, independent adult cat that’s used to being alone may be a good fit; a kitten or a cat that needs frequent attention or medical care probably isn’t. Before deciding, ask the current owner how the cat handles long stretches alone, what its daily routine looks like, and whether it has any health or behavior needs. Then look at your longest workdays, not your easiest ones: can you reliably make time for feeding, litter care, play, and companionship, and cover routine and unexpected vet bills?

It’s okay that coming home to an empty house is part of why you want a cat. Just let that feeling be a reason to explore adoption, not a reason to rush it. If the cat’s needs fit the life you have now, you don’t need to wait out some arbitrary mourning period. If they don’t, saying no now would be the same kind of care you showed your husky.

A little, for the joke—not for reconnecting with your mate or for secretly meaning what you said. “They don’t really live up to the hype” might be familiar banter to him, but it came right after you’d been talking about dates with **her**. It’s understandable that she heard it as “being with you is disappointing.” That doesn’t mean you were deliberately slagging her off, but explaining the joke doesn’t undo how it landed.

Give her some space tonight. Tomorrow, try an apology that doesn’t ask her to agree it was funny: “I meant it as a throwaway joke, but I can see why it sounded like I was putting you down to my mate. I’m sorry I made you the punchline. I’m happy with you.”

Separately, if she read your messages without permission, it’s fair to talk about phone privacy. You can own the joke without treating the snooping as okay, and you can raise the privacy issue without using it to cancel out the apology.

And you don’t have to make her your *only* focus to show you appreciate what she gave up to move. Having friendships of your own is healthy. The thing to fix here is the joke and how you two handle the hurt—not the fact that you’re talking to an old friend.

No, you wouldn’t be an asshole for adopting a cat three months after rehoming your husky. You made a hard decision based on what he needed, and you took care to find him a home where he’s happy. Adopting a cat wouldn’t undo that or mean you loved him any less.

The real question is whether **this particular cat** would do well with your schedule. A healthy adult cat with a history of being comfortable alone might be a good fit; a kitten, a cat that needs medication during the day, or one that gets distressed when left alone might not be. Ask the current owner how the cat handles long stretches alone, what its daily routine looks like, and whether it has any health or behavior needs. Then look at your longest workdays: can you reliably make time for play and attention, keep up with daily care, and afford routine and unexpected vet bills?

If those answers are reassuring, ask whether the owner would be open to a trial period with a clear plan for what happens if it doesn’t work out. If the cat’s needs or the costs don’t fit right now, it’s okay to pass. Missing the companionship is a good reason to consider adopting; it just doesn’t have to be the reason you say yes to this cat.

No, you wouldn’t be an asshole for adopting a cat three months after rehoming your dog. There’s no required waiting period. What matters is whether you can meet **this cat’s needs with the schedule and budget you have now**.

You made a painful decision when your circumstances changed, and it sounds like you took real care finding your husky a good home. You can be glad he’s thriving and still miss him every time you open the door. Wanting companionship again doesn’t take away from how much you loved him.

A healthy adult cat who’s used to being alone during the workday may be a better fit for your schedule than your husky was. But if you’re still out for 12-plus hours most days, I’d ask the current owner how this particular cat handles long stretches alone, how much interaction it seeks, and whether it has any medical or behavioral needs. Then look at what you can reliably offer even on your longest days: feeding, a clean litter box, play and attention, and room in your budget for routine and unexpected vet care.

I wouldn’t commit yet. Meet the cat and have a candid conversation about your schedule. If the cat’s needs fit what you can reliably provide, adopting could be a good choice. If they don’t, passing on this particular cat isn’t a verdict on you as a pet owner—it’s the same kind of care you showed your dog.

**NTA for being hurt.** You can respect your dad’s right to decide what happens to his money and still feel disappointed by what his decision seems to say. From your account, you spent years working in the family business and paid your own way through college while watching your dad support both your brothers. The equal split may sting less because of the dollar amount than because you want to know he noticed those differences.

But **an equal inheritance doesn’t necessarily mean your dad thinks everyone contributed equally or that your relationships are interchangeable**. He may see the will as a way to include all three of you, not as a final accounting of who worked more or who already received help. You don’t have to share his idea of fairness to respect it.

You were right to discourage your older brother from confronting him. I’d also stop discussing the split with your brother for now, especially given your role as executor. If you want to talk to your dad, first ask yourself: *If the will never changed, what would I still want him to hear?* If it’s that the years you worked together mattered to you, or that being independent sometimes left you feeling overlooked, you can talk about that without making your stepbrother the subject. And if your dad’s health makes this a bad time, it’s fine to sit with the feeling rather than act on it.

Wanting acknowledgment isn’t the same as demanding a bigger share. Keeping those two things separate is the best way to honor both your feelings and your dad’s wishes.

**NTA for stepping back.** Your friend knew how much you liked her, told you he wanted the night to go well for you two, and then spent it flirting with her. She was free to flirt with whoever she wanted, but you were also reasonable to expect more consideration from a close friend. Being drunk may explain his behavior; it doesn’t erase it.

His apology may have been sincere, but calling it “not that big a deal” after you explained why it hurt undercut it. At the same time, the old Tinder match and the new follows don’t prove he planned anything or that he’s pursuing her now. You don’t need to prove either to take the breach of trust seriously.

“I hate you” was harsh, and you can take that back if you regret it without taking back the boundary. You also don’t have to decide right now whether the friendship is over forever. “I was hurt and angry, and I need space” is enough. If you later want to see whether the friendship is repairable, pay attention to whether he can acknowledge what hurt you without arguing that you shouldn’t be hurt.

And you don’t necessarily have to give up your other friendships because he’s closer to the group. Reach out to people you want to keep seeing one-on-one. You can take space from him without asking anyone to pick a side.

No, you’re not an asshole for being hurt. And you were right to discourage your brother from confronting your dad. Feeling disappointed and trying to pressure your dad into changing his will are two very different things.

It sounds like the equal split may sting because of what it seems to say about your history: you spent years working in the family business and paid your own way through college, while your dad has given your stepbrother substantial financial support. It’s understandable to want your dad to recognize those differences. But an equal inheritance doesn’t necessarily mean he thinks you’ve all contributed equally or needed the same things from him. He may see the will as a way to include all three of you, not as a final accounting of who worked harder or who’s already received more. You don’t know how he weighed those things unless he tells you.

A useful question is: **If the split never changed, what would you still want your dad to know?** If the answer is that your years in the business mattered to you and you’d like to know they mattered to him, that’s a conversation you can have without making it about your stepbrother or the money. If what you mostly need right now is to vent, pick someone outside the inheritance rather than continuing to discuss it with your older brother, who already wants to confront your dad.

You can respect your dad’s wishes and carry them out faithfully as executor without having to feel good about them.

**NTA for being upset.** You can respect your dad’s right to divide his estate and still feel hurt by what the equal split seems to say. It sounds like you’re looking at the years you worked in the family business, the costs you covered yourself, and the support your dad has given both your brothers, and wondering whether he noticed what you contributed and what you handled on your own.

But an equal share isn’t necessarily your dad’s verdict on who worked hardest, treated him best, or needed the most help. He may see your stepbrother as one of his children after years of living together, even if you and your stepbrother don’t feel much like siblings. It’s also telling that your older brother’s equal share doesn’t seem to sting in quite the same way, despite the support he’s received. It may help to ask yourself whether the hurt is about past financial help, your place in your dad’s family, or some of both.

You were right to discourage a confrontation. I’d also stop discussing the details with your brothers: you learned them because your dad trusted you to be executor, and those conversations can quickly turn into pressure on him. If what you really want is acknowledgment, you can ask for that without asking him to change the will: “Working in the business was a big part of my life, and sometimes I wonder how you remember those years and what my work meant to you.”

You’re not an asshole for having the feeling. What matters is whether you use it to understand what you need from your dad while he’s here, or turn it into a contest over who deserves more.

**NTA for taking space.** Your friend knew you liked her, told you he wanted the night to go well for you two, and then flirted with her and split off with her. She was free to flirt back, but you can reasonably expect more consideration from a close friend who knew how you felt. Being drunk might explain his behavior; it doesn’t erase the impact. And telling you it was “not that big a deal” undercut his apology.

That said, “I hate you” was harsh, and you don’t have to make a permanent decision while the embarrassment is fresh. The old Tinder match and the new follows understandably make you wonder, but they don’t prove he planned anything or that he’s pursuing her now. You don’t need to prove either of those things to decide that what happened hurt your trust.

If the friendship has otherwise been good, give yourself a few days and see whether you want one sober conversation. You could say: “I regret saying I hate you. I’m still hurt by what happened, and when you told me I was overreacting, I felt like you weren’t hearing me. I need some space.” You can take back the insult without taking back the boundary. If he keeps minimizing it, or you no longer want to repair things, you’re allowed to walk away.

And you don’t have to give up your whole social circle. You can reach out to mutual friends individually and make plans without asking anyone to pick a side.

**NTA for taking space, and you wouldn’t be wrong to end the friendship if the trust is gone.** But you don’t have to make that decision—or give up your whole social circle—while you’re still hurt.

The issue isn’t that she owed you exclusivity. It’s that your close friend knew how much you liked her, told you he wanted the night to go well for you two, and then spent it flirting with her. It makes sense that you felt blindsided and embarrassed. Being drunk may explain why he doesn’t remember, but it doesn’t undo what happened. His apology is worth acknowledging; telling you that you were overreacting undercut it.

The old Tinder match and new follows understandably make you more suspicious, but they don’t establish that he planned this or that they’ll pursue anything. You don’t need to prove either to decide that what happened that night damaged your trust.

“I hate you” was harsh. If you regret saying it, you can take it back without taking back the boundary: “I was hurt and said something harsher than I meant. I still need space. What bothered me was that you knew how I felt, told me you had my back, and then flirted with her. When you called it stupid, I felt dismissed.” If you later want to see whether the friendship can be repaired, pay attention to whether he can acknowledge that without arguing that you shouldn’t care.

And you can keep seeing mutual friends one-on-one without asking anyone to pick sides. Ending or pausing one friendship doesn’t have to mean losing the rest.

**A mild YTA for how you handled it, not for looking out for your colleague.** A stream of comments about her looks can get old, especially when she has to stay polite at work. But from what you describe, the wife made one compliment and asked where she was from. Calling her out as inappropriate was a stronger response than the moment called for. A simple “Let’s get back to the medication” would have redirected things without putting either woman on the spot.

Your colleague’s polite reply doesn’t tell you whether she welcomed the comment or was just smoothing over an awkward moment. If you’re concerned, ask her privately: “I jumped in earlier without checking with you. How did that land? Would you like me to step in when comments like that happen, or would you rather handle them yourself?”

You don’t have to ignore comments that are sexual, persistent, or clearly unwelcome. But for an ambiguous one-off, a neutral redirect and a private check-in are usually more supportive than a public reprimand.

A bit, yes. You weren’t wrong to look out for your colleague, but calling the wife’s comment “irrelevant and inappropriate” was sharper than the situation seemed to warrant.

Repeated remarks about someone’s looks at work can get tiring, and “You’re too kind” could have been genuine appreciation or just a polite way to move on. But this one compliment, followed by a question, doesn’t by itself establish that the wife was objectifying her. You could have kept the focus on care without publicly correcting her: “Let’s get back to the medication.”

The most useful next step is to check in privately with the new nurse: “I jumped in yesterday. How did that land for you? If comments like that come up again, would you rather I redirect or let you handle it?” That gives her a say in how you support her. If a comment is sexual, persistent, or clearly unwelcome, a firmer boundary makes sense.

A bit, yes—not for looking out for your colleague, but for publicly rebuking the wife over a brief compliment. “You’re so beautiful” can be unwelcome at work, especially when someone hears comments about her appearance all day. But from what you describe, this particular comment wasn’t sexual or persistent, and nothing in the exchange called for an immediate reprimand. A simple “Let’s get back to the medication” would have redirected the conversation without making it awkward.

The new nurse’s smile doesn’t prove she was comfortable; nurses often respond politely to keep an interaction smooth. It also doesn’t mean she wanted you to step in. **YTA here—not because one bad joke makes you a bad partner, but because the joke made Amber’s OCD sound like a perk for you, and you dismissed her when she told you how it landed.**
